player.seasonOutlook: Tatis was limited to 102 games last season due to a stress reaction in his right femur. His production was an improvement over a down 2023 season, but it fell short of the lofty standards established over the first three years of his career. The main difference was a drop in power fueled by a slightly lower average exit velocity on flyballs, though his barrel rate was still 92nd percentile. Tatis ran less last season with only 11 steals in 14 tries, though it is encouraging that he was 3-for-3 in September after returning from the leg injury. After he stole a total of 54 bases on 62 attempts over his two seasons prior to last, it's reasonable to expect more running this season, putting the 26-year-old in the first-round discussion.

Although his six-year MLB career hasn't yet reached the stratospheric levels that his Hall of Fame father's did, Junior has had some impressive exploits in his own right. Guerrero's 2024 saw him set personal bests in batting average, doubles, contact and whiff rates. It was his third 30-HR campaign and the fourth year in a row with at least 94 RBI. His contact-quality metrics rate among the best in the game, as his Statcast expected batting average across the past four seasons (.303) is fifth-best (minimum 1,200 plate appearances). Plus, he has played in all but 12 Blue Jays games during that time. The primary thing holding Guerrero back from an early first-round valuation is his ground ball-oriented swing. If he could once again show the kind of lift he did during his 48-HR 2021, he'd contend for an MVP award.

It's not often you'll see a catcher deliver the kind of breakthrough 2023 season that Contreras had and then following it up with an even more productive campaign. The No. 1 catcher from that year's Player Rater, and second-best in fantasy points, the Brewers backstop not only led his position in both scoring formats in 2024, but finished 28th in fantasy points and 44th on the Player Rater overall. Maintaining the contact and plate-discipline gains he exhibited two years ago was key to this transformation, and Contreras' jump into the 91st percentile in hard-hit rate last season reflects his status as one of the position's best power sources. He mashes left-handed pitchers -- FYI daily leaguers -- and should be the first catcher off the board in all fantasy formats.

The Astros gave Altuve a vote of long-term confidence last February in the form of a five-year extension and he rewarded their continued faith with a 20-20 season, his first such season since 2017. Altuve earned his ninth All-Star selection with a .306 average and 14 homers in the first half before dipping to .277 and six, respectively, in the second half. The second baseman has always made the most of his talents and continues to take advantage of the Crawford Boxes in Houston, slugging more than 100 points higher at home versus on the road last season. Gone are the days of first-round value, but Altuve can still provide well-round production, with his greatest contributions at this stage coming in runs and batting average. Altuve, nearing his 35th birthday in May, has been mostly healthy in recent years outside of 2023 when he missed nearly half the season with thumb and oblique injuries.

Once a first-round stalwart, Bichette is coming off a terrible season ravaged by injuries. A .599 OPS after a three-year mark of .815 is especially troublesome, though a 43.5 percent hard-hit rate last season offers hope, as does a clean bill of health after finger surgery. At least doubling last season's 4.4 percent barrel rate is key, and plausible if healthy. Bichette's steals have fallen since he swiped 25 in 26 tries in 2021, but he did notch five bags in what amounts to half a season last year, so a return to double-digit pilfers is in play. By his own account, Bichette tried to be more selective and has vowed to return to a more free-swinging approach. The cost to learn if Bichette re-enters the circle of trust is nominal compared to the reward.

Fried finds himself pitching for a new organization after spending the last nine seasons in the Atlanta organization, as the Yankees gave Fried a sizable deal despite the time missed in 2023 with a forearm strain as well as the neuritis in his pitching elbow in the middle of the 2024 season. The left-hander's ability to limit homers will be tested at Yankee Stadium, but left-center field being forgiving to his particular approach -- at least on paper -- should help balance things out in his favor. Fried throws seven different pitch types to both righties and lefties which puts hitters into uncomfortable situations. His ability to keep hitters off balance is why he is elite at limiting hard contact and why his ERA has just once been above 3.25 in a full season of work. The only risk associated with Fried would be a recurrence of the forearm issue from 2023 as the skills are more than steady.

Recovery from Tommy John surgery cost Bautista the entirety of 2024, but baseball is expected to have its best reliever (at the time of the operation) back in time to close for the Orioles come Opening Day. In 2023, he registered the sixth-best strikeout rate (46.4%) of any pitcher with at least 60 IP, and became only the eighth pitcher in history with at least 30 saves, 110 strikeouts and a sub-1.50 ERA. Whether Bautista's raw stuff will approach those heights in his first season back following surgery is a fair question, but perhaps his spring training might provide some hints. All signs point to his being worthy of a top-five selection at his position in fantasy leagues regardless.

Suzuki's name has been mentioned in trade rumors, but the Cubs' asking price is high and justifiably so given he has been well above league average at the plate in each of his three seasons in the majors. Suzuki spent time on the injured list again last season and saw his strikeout rate increase, but he kept his batting average over .280 and reached 20 homers for the second straight year. Taking advantage of the bigger bases and new rules limiting pickoff attempts, Suzuki went from six steals in 2023 to 16 last season. The reason the Cubs are willing to listen at all is his defense in the outfield, which was so shaky that the team decided to move him to designated hitter down the stretch. However, Suzuki has said that he does not want to be a full-time DH, which leaves open questions about his future. No matter where he ends up, Suzuki will be in the lineup nearly every day in 2025 since his bat is too good to keep on the bench.

While Ryan has established himself as a quality starting pitcher in Major League Baseball, injuries have delayed the full-on breakout. He went down in August with a Grade 2 teres major strain and never made it back onto the field last season, though the Twins said in November that Ryan was making good progress in his recovery. A groin injury derailed his 2023 season, but through it all the right-hander has made 79 starts over the past three seasons (31st in the majors in that span). His flyball tendencies make him susceptible to homers, but Ryan is stingy with walks and misses bats at an above-average clip with his five-pitch mix. More cautious players will want to wait and see how Ryan looks in the spring before jumping in with both feet while those with a higher level of risk tolerance should be eager to invest in the skills.

His status as a shortstop/closer during his college days at Nebraska, coupled with the 2021 Tommy John surgery that delayed the start of his professional career, perhaps allowed Schwellenbach to sneak beneath the radar entering 2024. The Braves, desperate for rotation options, gave him a look in late May, despite his having only made two starts as high as Double-A ball at the time. He never looked back. Schwellenbach finished 16th among starting pitchers in fantasy points, thanks to his five solid pitch offerings and an elite walk rate (his 4.6% ranked in the 95th percentile). While he's likely to regress somewhat as the league becomes more familiar with him, he has the skills to remain a top-40 fantasy starter if given the innings (he totaled 168 2/3 between the majors and minors in 2024).

Paredes was traded twice in the final sixth months of 2024, first to the Cubs and later to the Astros in the Kyle Tucker deal. The power dipped after his move from Tampa Bay to the North Side, but his new home in Houston looks like a great fit for Paredes' pull-heavy approach from the right side. Indeed the Crawford Boxes could help Paredes return to the 30-homer plateau, but a career .245 BABIP saddles him with a low batting average and speaks to his limited running ability. His batted-ball profile is not what one might expect, though Paredes is a unique player and the rules don't always apply to a hitter with his spray chart. The third baseman carries bonus first-base eligibility in leagues with a 15-game minimum.

Ray's rehab from May 2023 Tommy John surgery extended into late July, and from there, he managed to make just seven starts before being shut down in late August with a strained hamstring. Ray threw 30.2 innings with 43 punchouts and 15 walks, along with six homers. His velocity returned to 2021 levels and his path looks typical for a pitcher recovering from TJS -- the strikeouts come back first, and then command and control. Ray struggles with home runs, making it all the more important that he limit the free passes. His home venue is ideal for streaming, but it may be best to wait and gauge his health and command in the spring before investing.

Edman spent the first four months of the 2024 campaign on the injured list as he recovered from offseason wrist surgery and didn't see game action until after being traded from the Cardinals to the Dodgers at the deadline. The utility man played in 37 games during the regular season and had a .237/.294/.417 slash line with six homers and six steals, but he got on track during the playoffs with an .862 OPS in 67 plate appearances. Edman then inked a five-year extension with Los Angeles early in the offseason and he is expected to serve as the club's primary center fielder in 2025, though he'll likely still see some time at other positions. He's spent most of his career playing second base and shortstop, but he may be limited to outfield eligibility to begin the season since he made just one appearance at second base and 18 at shortstop last year. Edman averaged 12 home runs, 30 steals, 85 runs and 53 RBI across the three seasons prior to 2024, and that type of production is likely a best-case scenario in his age-30 campaign.

Senga's sophomore season in MLB never really got off the ground, as a shoulder strain put him on the shelf to begin the campaign and he strained his calf in his very first start back in July, costing him the rest of the regular season. He returned to make three appearances in the postseason, including a surprise start in Game 1 of the NLCS, pitching a total of five innings. That should have set the right-hander up for a relatively normal offseason, though workload expectations will be difficult to pin down after the lost year. He was able to overcome a high walk rate in his first season with the Mets after the making the jump from Japan. If healthy in 2025, Senga could continue to outperform the estimators thanks to the quality of his repertoire and the league's general discombobulation with his ghost forkball.

Considering the number of injuries that dogged him -- elbow trouble that cost him the first six weeks, forearm discomfort that cost him a June start, and a hamstring strain that sidelined him for 2 1/2 weeks in July -- Woo's 2024, which earned him a top-30 SP valuation in roto formats, was rather surprising. He has some of the best control in baseball, his 2.8% walk rate was best in baseball among those with at least 100 IP, and he had a 2.95 ERA over his last 29 big-league starts. Still, Woo's elbow and forearm issues raise future concerns about his durability. Monitor him carefully during spring training, but with better injury luck, he should deliver top-50 fantasy SP value.

Though he disappointed during a 2023 cup of coffee, Cowser quickly emerged as a bona fide MLB regular in the early stages of his rookie 2024, swatting six homers across an 11-game stretch in April to effectively lock himself into a starting role (131-of-153 Orioles games) the rest of the way. His power metrics were all well above-average, though his penchant for strikeouts threatens streakiness and a low batting average in 2025. Cowser should again serve as the team's starting left fielder and a heart-of-the-order bat -- a good place to be in a lineup chock full of long-term upside. He's a mid-to-late round value.

Witt followed up his sizzling, 2023 second-half breakthrough with a 2024 that might have garnered him an MVP award (not to mention top placement on our fantasy leaderboards), if not for Shohei Ohtani and Aaron Judge. Witt became the first player to manage multiple 30/30 seasons before his 25th birthday, and the 11th shortstop of any age with a 30/30 campaign. He led the majors in batting average, and was one of only six players with at least 100 runs scored and 100 RBI. Witt is one of the game's few true five-category rotisserie superstars, his combination of solid contact and extra-base ability affording him the chance to challenge for the fantasy points leaderboard. Plus, he's still only 24 years old. If there's a nit to pick, it's that he attempted only 15 steals across his most recent 94 games (playoffs included), which could be as much small sample size noise as it might signal his seeing more red lights on the bases as his bat becomes more critical to the Royals' competitive chances.

Turner was limited to 121 games last season as a left hamstring strain cost him a bit over six weeks in May and June. He continues to be productive on the wrong side of 30, though anyone so reliant on his legs takes on a little more risk with each season. Turner's sprint speed registered in the 96th percentile in 2024, so the league's smoothest slider still has wheels. Turner's quality of contact is around league average, so he needs speed to continue to be among the league leaders in infield hits. Last season, Turner stole 10 bases in 33 games before getting hurt, but then he swiped just four bags in the subsequent 63 contests after returning before adding five more over his final 25 games, with the lull in the middle was likely due to protecting his hamstring. Turner is no longer among the elite shortstops, but he heads up the next tier.

In almost any other year, Merrill's 2024 breakthrough would have secured him a Rookie of the Year Award. He became only the fifth rookie in history with at least a .290 batting average, 20 HR, 90 RBI and 15  SB. The previous four all took home top rookie honors (Orlando Cepeda 1958, Nomar Garciaparra 1997, Carlos Beltran 1999, Ryan Braun 2007). Tuck that away if Merrill's value in your draft remotely softens, especially in light of his late-season skills improvement, as he hit .314/.349/.596 with 7% more fly balls after the All-Star break than before it. He no longer carries shortstop eligibility, but that doesn't make him any less attractive of an outfield pick in the early rounds. In keeper leagues, Merrill is a building block.

Elbow inflammation put Valdez on the shelf early on last year, but he made a quick recovery and ended up totaling 176.1 innings during the 2024 regular season, pitching to a stellar 2.91 ERA and 1.11 WHIP. The left-hander has never been the most dominant arm in terms of strikeouts, but he generates groundballs at an incredibly high clip -- over 60 percent for his career -- mostly on the strength of his sinking fastball. High whiff rates on his secondaries suggest there may be some untapped strikeout potential, though Valdez is already 31 years old and paying for another level would be ill advised. Valdez leads the majors in wins with 44 over the past three seasons and will be in position to reach double digits for the Astros once again before potentially hitting free agency next winter.

Be it by design or happenstance, Schwarber's groundball rate last year was his highest in a full season since 2018. Coupled with a career-high hard-hit rate on grounders, Schwarber posted the second-best batting average of his career. His power dipped, but Schwarber's 38 homers were still the eighth most in MLB last season and his quality of contact remained elite. The overall improvement stemmed from hitting southpaws better than right-handers for the first time in his career. Splits like this are often anomalies, so expect regression as Schwarber's platoon splits likely revert to career levels. Keep in mind too that drafting Schwarber means locking up the utility spot since he has lost outfield eligibility entering 2025.

Webb continues to be one of the game's most durable and reliable starters, despite fanning hitters at a below-average clip. Control and command remain Webb's bread and butter, along with an extreme groundball rate. His 613 innings since 2022 lead the majors, but his 529 strikeouts over that span rank 15th. Webb's ERA and WHIP are both top 10 among all starters with at least 500 innings over the past three seasons, but both are vulnerable to variance since Webb allows so many balls in play. Feeding into the concern is the fact that Webb's swinging-strike rate has declined each of the past three seasons. Accepting the low strikeout discount on Webb has been a fruitful endeavor, but it's reached the point where doing so invites more risk than may be evident by recent performance.

Whereas most catchers wear down rather quickly due the rigors of the position, Perez is still running strong at nearly 35 years old. He exceeded 100 RBI last season for the second time in his career and surged past 20 homers once again en route to his fifth Silver Slugger Award. Perez is the active leader in games played at catcher and 58th on the all-time list. The Royals have made a concerted effort to limit Perez's time behind the plate in recent years, giving him more time at first base and DH, which makes all the sense in the world given the mileage on Perez's knees and with Freddy Fermin proving plenty capable of helping with the workload. Perez is firmly in the old-and-boring category, but his track record of power production from the catcher spot should keep his services in high demand in fantasy baseball.

Reynolds is a textbook Professional Hitter coming off four straight 20-homer seasons and back-to-back 20-10 campaigns. His batting average has not fallen below .260 in a full season and Reynolds has been an All-Star in two of the past four years since his fluke down year in 2020. While his defense in the outfield corners has fallen off a cliff, the Pirates have not seemed to mind nor have they indicated a positional change could be in the cards. Reynolds signed an eight-year contract extension in 2023 and will return to anchor the heart of the Pittsburgh order after batting exclusively out of the two hole last season -- typically where teams put their best hitter. Entering his age-30 season, Reynolds provides a stable floor in terms of skills and playing time.

After giving up eight earned runs over 1.1 innings in his 2024 debut, Ober went on an incredible run in which he went 12-4 with a 3.05 ERA and 0.92 WHIP over 138.1 innings, before hitting the skids again at the end of the season. Overall, it was an impressive showing for the 6-foot-9 righty as he solidified his standing in the middle of the Minnesota rotation. He has four quality pitches and his strikeout and walk rates are good enough to make up for the occasional bout of gopheritis. The disappointing end to the season (0-4, 5.59 ERA in his final seven starts) may be enough to keep the more casual drafters away, but the secret is out amongst the wider drafting public. Chances are, the home runs will persist given his flyball tendencies, but Ober is good enough to overcome them and reach double-digit wins once again for a competitive Twins team.

Tasked with taking over the No. 1 starter role for Milwaukee following Corbin Burnes' departure via trade, Peralta performed admirably in 2024, albeit not quite to the level of his ace predecessor. His strikeout and walk rates went in the wrong direction and he had some issues with the long ball, particularly at home, allowing 1.72 HR/9 at American Family Field. Peralta also had trouble the third time through the order, posting a 7.52 ERA, a far cry from the 3.86 mark he posted the third time through in 2023. Nonetheless, he reached double-digit wins for the third time in four seasons as the Brewers ran away with the NL Central. While he may be miscast as an ace, Peralta has reached 30 starts and 200 strikeouts in back-to-back seasons. He totaled a career-high 173.2 innings last year and will be a bargain for the team at an $8 million price tag for 2025.

Defense doesn't count in fantasy baseball scoring, but Crow-Armstrong's highlight reel glovework helps keep his bat in the lineup. He hits the ball with more authority than others that are reliant on steals for fantasy purposes, but he strikes out more and lacks patience. Crow-Armstrong also hits more fly balls than a typical speed merchant. A lot must come together, but Crow-Armstrong has the makings of a fantasy star, though that's not likely in 2025. He must first learn to make better swing decisions, so he can best blend his power and speed potential. For now, consider Crow-Armstrong a source of cheap steals, but be prepared to absorb a low batting average.

The 2022 version of Gimenez would have been an outstanding fit for Toronto because that version of Gimenez provided one thing absent in most of the Toronto lineups that year -- on-base percentage. Gimenez reached base 37 percent of the time that season while the collective group who hit leadoff for the Jays in 2024 had a .297 on-base percentage. Alas, Gimenez has not come close to replicating that career year from 2022. Gimenez is an impatient hitter who is looking to put the best pitch possible into play and leverage his speed on the basepaths. He has the seventh-fewest walks among all hitters with at least 1500 plate appearances since 2022, but he is also ninth overall among that same group in steal attempts. That's the skill Toronto will be leaning on in 2025 to help bolster the bottom of the lineup.

Rengifo was not in the Opening Day lineup for the Angels last season and ended up making three separate trips to the injured list, which kept him 80 games played. First he dealt with a viral infection that caused painful blisters on his feet, while wrist trouble shelved him on the other two occasions. Despite those issues, Rengifo swiped 24 bags in 31 attempts, showing an entirely new level with his speed after he had previously topped out at six steals in a season. He also hit an even .300 during his time on the field, up close to 40 points from 2023, though it's difficult to fully buy into either new element of his game given the sample size and Rengifo's performance history. That said, Rengifo has more pop than he showed last season, and while he is no longer quad-eligible like he was entering 2024, he still qualifies at third base and second base, providing valuable flexibility.

Hoskins' first season away Philadelphia did not exactly go as planned, and the 2023 layoff due to his recovery from ACL surgery certainly did not help matters. The old saying goes, "hitting is timing and pitching is about the disruption of timing," and while Hoskins still got to enjoy familiar National League pitching, the long layoff was a major disruptor of timing. That said, his strikeout rate has ticked up each of the past four seasons, so it's a trend that goes beyond last year. Hoskins has not lost the ability to barrel up a baseball, but his ability to hit fastballs is showing cracks, as his batting average against fastballs has gone from .287 in 2018 down to .241 last season. He will be 32 when the 2025 season begins and will be aiming to rebuild his numbers to the point where his agent advises him to decline his $18 million mutual option for 2026.

Signed by the Royals at the end of January, Estevez figures to battle Lucas Erceg, primarily, for saves to begin 2025, and his eight-digit salary probably gives him a leg up in that competition. Estevez managed a career-best 27.8% strikeout rate in his first full season as a closer in 2023, then added enough gains in terms of control last year to serve as a competent, well above-average closer. Fantasy managers will want to monitor the Royals' bullpen pecking order through the Cactus League schedule -- saves carry a three-point advantage over holds in ESPN standard leagues -- but regardless of role, Estevez is a reliever well worth taking in the late rounds.

It is perplexing to look at Nootbaar's production over three full seasons because we are left wanting more. His strikeout and walk rates are better than average and all measures shows he makes quality contact with the baseball. Yet, Nootbaar has never hit more than 14 homers in a season and has yet to drive in 50 runs in a season. This speaks to Nootbaar's biggest weakness: staying on the field. He and the injured list have been thick as thieves and 2024 saw them spend time together due to a rib fracture and an oblique injury. Nootbaar would be a great fit for higher in the lineup with another team, but St. Louis projects him to hit in the lower half as things stand right now. Maybe this will be the year Nootbaar stays healthy and stays in the lineup enough to put up the type of numbers his overall profile suggests are hiding somewhere, but history says otherwise.

After teasing fantasy managers for years with encouraging underlying metrics but so-so results, a tweak to his mechanics in late July finally spawned a breakthrough for Manaea. By lowering his arm angle, he added three full percentage points to his whiff rate and 6% to his ground-ball percentage across his final 12 regular-season starts, during which he had three double-digit strikeout games, a 3.09 ERA, a 28.4% K rate and the second-most fantasy points among pitchers (202). Whether Manaea can maintain those gains is a fair question as he had never before 2024 posted a full-season ERA lower than 3.50, but there's certainly top-40 SP potential here with the tweaks taken into account. He's worth a quick spring re-examination before investing at that price point, but his arrow is pointing upward.

Even at age 38, Santana continues to be one of the better points-league values in fantasy drafts. He's only the sixth player in history to have managed at least a 10% batting title-eligible walk rate in 14 straight seasons and he's the only active player with at least an 80% contact rate and 800 walks (he has 1,278). That polished plate approach continues to earn Santana regular at-bats, which is what he should receive back in Cleveland, as the Guardians' 1B replacement for Josh Naylor. Even in the waning years of Santana's career, he's a high-floor, mid-to-late round value in mixed leagues.

After teasing a late-career power surge in 2023, Diaz reverted to his previous power levels last season. Overall, Diaz continues to sport elite quality of contact metrics, but since he hits grounders more than half of the time, he is unable to take full advantage. Not only did Diaz's power drop, but his batting average with runners in scoring position fell 90 points, limiting his RBI. After carrying a double-digit walk rate over the previous five seasons, Diaz's patience waned last season, leaving him with the second-lowest OBP of his career. Diaz is best suited for points leagues, where his high doubles total can help mitigate fewer homers. Look for a rebound, but 2023 will likely go down as Diaz's career year.

A shin contusion that later revealed a small fracture, costing the right fielder 79 games, might be the one thing holding Tucker back from entering 2025 as one of fantasy baseball's most prominent superstars. At the time of the injury, caused by his fouling a pitch off his shin, he was on pace for a 50/27 season and 112 runs scored, continuing his pattern as one of baseball's most reliable five-category rotisserie performers. Tucker returned in September with a flourish, batting .365 with four homers across 18 games, giving confidence that he should resume in 2025 where he left off in his walk year with his new team, the Cubs. In fact, he might have room to grow, considering 2024 saw him set new personal bests with his 16.5% walk, 17.5% chase, 41.3% fly ball and 12.9% Barrel rates.

Few players hit the baseball with greater authority than Alvarez. Across six MLB seasons, his 53.2% Statcast hard-hit rate is third-best (minimum 1,000 plate appearances), his 93.5 mph average exit velocity is sixth-best and his 17.1% Barrel rate is seventh-best. He's one of only five players with 30-plus homers in each of the past four seasons and, among those five, his .296 batting average trails only Aaron Judge's .300. Alvarez's main differentiators from the game's elite are his injury history -- he has made seven trips to the IL  -- and a lack of hardware, statistical records or a big free-agent contract. That might, however, make him a relative discount among players who deserve selection during the first two rounds.

Riley entered 2024 as one of the most consistent hitters in baseball with three straight 30-homer, 90-RBI seasons and an .878 OPS during that span, but he underwhelmed last year with a .256/.322/.461 slash line and 19 home runs through 110 games before a fractured hand ended his campaign in mid-August. Despite the drop in production, the veteran third baseman was still making consistent hard contact, which bodes well for a rebound in 2025. He should have a fairly typical offseason given the timing of the injury, so there's no real question on his status heading into spring training. Riley's .783 OPS in a down season illustrates his high floor, and there's a strong likelihood he bounces back to his All-Star form in 2025 given his track record and the fact he'll turn just 28 years old in April.

A popular preseason pick for 2024 AL Rookie of the Year honors, Langford instead struggled mightily in his first taste of the majors, batting just .227/.287/.300 with only seven extra-base hits across his first 40 games. As many a rookie has done before, however, he picked up the pace from there, culminating in June AL Rookie of the Month and September AL Player and Rookie of the Month honors. For the season as a whole, Langford's metrics were well above-average across the board, giving hope that the superstardom predicted for him at this point one year ago remains his future track. He should not be allowed to linger too deep into the middle rounds of any draft.

The centerpiece of the 2023-24 offseason's Juan Soto trade, King proved every bit as capable a starting pitcher across 30 starts for the Padres last season as he was over an eight-start stint for the Yankees to conclude 2023. In fact, King was one of only four pitchers to strike out at least 200 batters with a sub-3.00 ERA, joining both Cy Young Award winners (Chris Sale, Tarik Skubal) and Zack Wheeler. He only strengthened his underlying numbers over the season's second half, getting a whiff nearly one-third of the time hitters swung at any of his pitches. It sets up the right-hander well for a similarly productive 2025, albeit with some risk of ERA regression, as his Statcast xERA should be nearly three-quarters of a run higher. Still, that's a top-20 capable fantasy starter regardless of format.

Consistency is tough to find in the late innings. Even the greats like Hader endure some statistical variance -- he had a 5.22 ERA in a difficult 2022 season -- and it comes with the territory of facing the best hitters in the world in the highest-leverage spots night after night. Hader tallied 34 saves in his first year with Houston and has now racked up 30-plus saves in each of the last five full MLB seasons. The left-hander occasionally toes the line with walks and home runs, but his sinking fastball and swing-and-miss slider form a highly effective 1-2 punch. While the Astros have done some retooling this winter, but there is little reason to think Hader won't be the closer for Houston in 2025, with the flexibility and dominance to exceed 100 strikeouts in relief.

DeGrom has managed to put up just 197.1 innings over the past four seasons due to his body constantly failing him, which is a shame considering he's one of the best pitchers of this generation. The right-hander last worked a full season in 2019 when he pitched his third consecutive season of 200-plus innings while winning his second consecutive Cy Young Award. He made it back for three starts at the end of 2024 and essentially picked up where he left off with 14 strikeouts and one walk over those outings. This remains the ultimate risk/reward pick because at least Tyler Glasnow is good for 100-plus innings in a season around his injuries while deGrom has barely worked 100 innings over the previous three seasons combined. Even 100 innings of deGrom brilliance would be more valuable to a roster than 150 innings of another arm, but expecting that sort of workload might be optimistic.

Iglesias and Atlanta has been a match made in heaven, as he's posted a 1.96 ERA and 0.92 WHIP in 151.1 innings spanning 152 appearances over the past two and a half seasons. He shaved his WHIP to just 0.74 last season and reached the 30-save threshold for the fifth time in his career. Iglesias lost a little bit off his strikeout rate and benefited from a .199 BABIP, but that's picking nits. All four of his pitches had BAAs under .180 and he went without allowing an earned run for about half the season from mid-June to mid-September. Now 35 years old, Iglesias will be pitching for a big payday next winter in the final year of his deal. There's always a chance he could be dealt if Atlanta falls out of contention, but the right-hander enters the year with a ton of job security in his current situation.

Oblique, shoulder and rib injuries cost him the final month of 2023 and the entirety of 2024, but McLain returned to action during the Arizona Fall League and delivered .240/.356/.520 rates while seeing time at three different positions (2B, 3B and CF). He'll be ready to compete for a utility role this spring and, with a strong March, should be ready to pick up where he last left off -- as a potential 25/25 player. McLain does have a lot of swing-and-miss in his game, putting him at risk for slumps and a low batting average, but he's an attractive mid-round pick, with slightly more appeal in rotisserie than points-based leagues.

Munoz enters the 2025 season in a slightly different situation from just one year ago. He was not the clearcut favorite for the primary closer role last spring after the acquisition of Gregory Santos from the White Sox as well as the impressive work from Matt Brash in 2023. Yet, Munoz was the last man standing and he is now the clear frontrunner for saves in Seattle. He managed to avoid the injured list last season despite dealing with some back issues, earning an appearance in the All-Star Game. Munoz has twice now posted ERAs below 2.50 and WHIPs below 1.00 in the past three seasons, and the outstanding Seattle rotation and suspect offense almost ensure that there will be many late and close opportunities for Munoz to finally get to 30 saves in 2025.

No longer is Gallen being drafted as a borderline ace. He missed roughly a month of the 2024 season with a hamstring injury and his walk rate increased by more than three percentage points, which led to his WHIP jumping from 1.12 to 1.26. Gallen's knuckle curve remains an excellent put-away pitch, but his four-seam fastball and slider were entirely hittable last season. Perhaps Gallen has fallen further than he should. After all, the right-hander was a Cy Young finalist in the National League in 2023, he won 14 games in a down year and still does a lot well relative to most starting pitchers in MLB, including limiting homers. Take the name away and the underlying profile is not all that exciting, but Gallen's numbers over the last three years give him a case to be viewed as a third or fourth starter in fantasy entering 2025.

Walker has been in the San Francisco system since being drafted out of Washington State in 2018. He made the slow climb up the organizational ladder as a reliever and finally made the big-league roster in 2023. This past season was the coming-out party, as Walker ended up as the primary closer for the Giants by the end of the season and was one of just two relievers to make at least 75 appearances and work at least 80 innings in 2024. While most pitchers have taken a step backward historically after such a season, Walker could pull a Brad Hand from 2016 and 2017 and repeat his success. Walker's delivery and stuff make it very tough for hitters to square him up, and with the closer job in hand, the right-hander is in great shape for 25-plus saves in 2025.

?The Martian? figures to take over starting left field duties for the Yankees in 2025 and, while his defense often came into question during a late-season audition last year, his Triple-A dominance in 2023-24 (.325/.391/.495 rates, 7 HR, 18 SB in 53 games) reflects his immense offensive potential. Dominguez is one of the more important hitters to watch during spring training, as more patience and more lift in his swing than he showed in his two cups of coffee with the Yankees could do him a world of good. He should be a good source of stolen bases at the very least, a back-of-the-roster mixed-league player at the median, and a breakthrough player with building-block dynasty potential at his best.

Neto broke out last season to the tune of 23 homers and 30 steals in 155 games for the Angels. Despite that, the fantasy world is treating the shortstop with some trepidation entering his age-24 season in 2025. Most pertinently, his availability for the start of the upcoming season is uncertain after he underwent right shoulder surgery in November. Neto was also caught stealing 10 times and managed just a .697 OPS against right-handed pitching. The concerns are valid, but Neto improved his OBP and SLG significantly in the second half and his playing time will be locked in once he completes his recovery from surgery. His batted-ball profile leaves a lot to be desired, but this kind of power-speed combo is tough to find outside of the early rounds, even if it is largely volume driven.

Ruiz had a bout with the flu early on last season which cost him multiple weeks and caused him to lose nearly 20 pounds. In the end, his OPS fell by nearly 100 points from 2023, though he rebounded a bit in the second half, and it's fair to wonder how much the influenza and subsequent weight loss affected his play. Part of the Nationals' return from the Dodgers in the 2021 Trea Turner-Max Scherzer trade, Ruiz has not quite developed as expected, offensively or defensively. Ruiz makes consistent contact at the plate and packs some power, but a low walk rate drags down his OBP. Signed to a long-term extension in March of 2023, Ruiz will have every chance to rebound and continue his maturation as a player, but at 26 years old, the clock is ticking for him to prove he can make it as a No. 1 catcher.

Eovaldi went a long way in shedding the fragility label by throwing his second-highest innings total last season. He will miss a start from time to time, as he has but twice made 30 starts, but when he is out there, he works deep into games thanks to his ability to throw four different pitches to lefties and five to righties. The repertoire is a bit susceptible to the long ball, but Eovaldi's stinginess with walks offsets the damage from those homers. He is one of just six pitchers to have posted an ERA of 4.00 and a WHIP below 1.25 while pitching at least 100 innings in each of the past four seasons, joining the likes of Framber Valdez, Corbin Burnes, Kevin Gausman, Logan Webb and Zack Wheeler. That's good company to keep.

Soler was moved to the Angels in the offseason, which may allow him to mimic the career path Marcell Ozuna has taken the past two seasons in Atlanta. Soler and Ozuna share a similar profile in that both are known for their hard contact at the plate as well as the hard contact off their iron gloves in the outfield. Ozuna's career resurgence came about once Atlanta threw him in to the full-time designated hitter role and let him flourish, and Soler now has that same opportunity with the Angels that he was never going to have with Atlanta. Soler's strikeout rate has been better in recent seasons, but it's still worse than average, and that combined with his slow speed puts a hard cap on his batting average. Still, the power and run production could be surprisingly useful.

Busch, a first-round pick by the Dodgers in 2019, was traded to the Cubs last winter, opening up a path to playing time at the major-league level. Busch took advantage and showed what he's made of with an above-average offensive season at age 26 that included 21 homers and a .775 OPS across 567 plate appearances. Best of all for his 2025 outlook, Busch handled same-side pitching capably, slashing .258/.330/.382 against left-handed pitching. That performance along with his defense at first base, which the Cubs see as Gold Glove caliber, figure to keep Busch in the lineup nearly every day. First base has become rather top heavy in fantasy baseball and Busch makes for a decent fallback option for those that end up waiting at the position.

Bassitt's ERA last year was half a run higher than the previous season, while his 1.46 WHIP in 2024 was the second highest among qualified starters. Bassitt's walk rate was his highest since 2018, but the bigger culprit was a .333 BABIP, third highest among all qualifiers. A bloated hit rate can be misfortune, but it can also be a sign of a pitcher being more hittable. Bassitt's strikeout rate is a tick below league average, so he needs to minimize traffic to be effective. Bassitt's track record warrants the benefit of the doubt, but he'll be 36 years old this season, so a full rebound will be challenging. Pitching in the AL East isn't conducive to favorable matchups, relegating Bassitt to deep leagues, at least until he demonstrates a return to his previous control levels.

This is the Lowe whose name rhymes with "ow," reflecting his six trips to the IL across the past three seasons alone, for back (three), triceps, knee and oblique issues, totaling 162 missed Rays games. Between the absences, Lowe has continued to show elite-to-top-shelf raw power metrics, and his 5.2% home run rate across the last five seasons leads all second basemen. That ability makes him too good to completely ignore in mixed leagues, though selecting him demands a strong backup plan.

Taillon had a surprising return to his halcyon days this past season, winning 12 of his 28 starts and pitching to the best ERA of his career. No new pitch was added nor was any one pitch thrown that much more than it was in 2023, but the sweeper performed better in 2024. Taillon does what many pitchers without big fastballs do, choosing to throw six different pitches rather than honing in on a smaller collection of pitches. He usually manages to keep hitters off-balance by throwing four of his six offerings at least 15 percent of the time. He continued to lag in the strikeout department last season -- his strikeout rate was several clicks below the league average for starting pitchers -- so he will have to continue to rely upon batted-ball fortunes to keep his ERA out of the danger zone.

What toe problem? Judge, who missed 42 games after tearing a ligament in his right big toe crashing into an outfield wall in June 2023, entered 2024 facing legitimate questions about future maintenance of the ailment. Instead, he delivered a season for the ages: MLB-leading numbers in home runs, RBIs, walks (133), OBP (.458), slugging (.701), OPS (1.159), OPS-plus (223) and Wins Above Replacement (10.8). Oh, yes, and a career-high 158 games played. Judge's contact-quality metrics are off the charts -- he has paced the majors in expected wOBA, Barrel and hard-hit rates among hitters with at least as many plate appearances as his in each of the past three seasons -- and he's among the game's most selective hitters, even if his game has lots of swing-and-miss. There aren't many more well-rounded players to select with a first-round fantasy draft pick.

Amidst a bevy of talented, fastball-throwing frontline starters in Seattle, Gilbert has quietly emerged as a prospective ace. He has made noticeable gains in numerous statistical categories over the past two seasons, including WHIP, walk, strikeout, whiff and ground ball rates. Plus, he has cut roughly a half a run from his Statcast expected ERA in both of those campaigns. Gilbert's addition of a splitter in 2023 helped him become a more strikeout-oriented starter, and his move to a six-pitch repertoire with less fastball reliance in 2024 helped further diversify his skill set. While the Mariners offense probably hasn't improved to the point that he'll significantly boost last year's nine wins, Gilbert should again deliver excellent numbers otherwise. He's a solid fantasy building block.

In 2024, many things went just right for Chisholm, a power/speed rotisserie gem for fantasy managers (albeit one with a penchant for injuries). He boosted his contact rate, improving his month-over-month consistency at the plate, played a career-best 147 games, and flourished following a midseason trade to the Yankees, batting .275/.325/.500 with 11 homers and 18 steals in 46 regular-season games in pinstripes. What's more, Chisholm adapted nicely to his new role at third base in New York, and his projected status as their second baseman to begin 2025 might quickly make him eligible at three positions. He might always be at risk of missing time with future ailments, but he's in a great spot for above-average power and elite speed, a combination that gives him top-50 overall upside in rotisserie formats. Bear in mind, however, that Chisholm's value in points-based and sabermetric scoring is a couple of tiers below that.

Abrams appeared in only 138 games last season, but half of the missed time occurred in September when he missed out on the last eight games of the season after being demoted to Triple-A for staying out all night prior to a day game. Despite a second-half swoon, Abrams improved his hard-hit rate overall and experienced an uptick in power. The added production helped mitigate a drop in steals. In 2023, Abrams swiped 47 bags in 51 tries for an outstanding 92 percent success rate. Last season, he was just 31-for-43 (72 percent). Still just 24 years old, Abrams is expected to learn from last season's disciplinary action and continue maturing as a person and player. The arrows are pointing upward, especially if he can cut down on last season's caught stealing number.

Rutschman's smooth, year-over-year ascent to the top of the fantasy catcher rankings hit a roadblock last June. Through his first 77 games, he was batting .300/.351/.480 with 15 home runs and was the top-scoring fantasy catcher. After being struck on the hand with a foul tip, however, he hit just .189/.279/.280 with four homers over his final 71 games. Given the injury, it's rational to forgive Rutschman for the sluggish finish. Even though his spring training bears closer watching than usual, he's a prime-age 27 after being the No. 1 overall pick in the 2019 amateur draft. He has drawn rave reviews from scouts for years, so it's easy to make the case that Rutschman remains a fantasy building block and a sound early-round pick regardless of format.

Oh, what his 2024 season might have been had he come to contract terms before March 19. Snell struggled to get up to speed across the season's first three months, spending time on the IL due to adductor and groin issues, but once he found his groove, he managed a 1.23 ERA, a 38.1% strikeout rate and the majors' most fantasy points across his final 14 starts. Snell does have a history of statistical peaks over seasonal portions rather than the whole, but he also possesses multiple Cy Young Awards (2018, 2023), and his second-best-in-baseball 2.82 ERA (minimum 300 innings) across the past three seasons points to him likely being at an overall high point. The Dodgers should do well managing his workload and getting the most out of him, and there's a very real chance that Snell will rebound to rank among his position's best performers.

Yelich's troublesome back finally forced him under the knife in August, ending his season. Specifically, the procedure was a microdiscectomy, a spinal surgery to remove part or all of a bulging or herniated disc. While Yelich was still not cleared to swing a bat as of mid-December, the team is expecting him to be ready early on in spring training. The outfielder produced at a high level in between IL stints last season, slashing .315/.406/.504 with 11 homers and 21 steals in just 73 games. The back now being surgically repaired offers hope that Yelich could stay on the field and return to something close to his previous levels of production, though it would be unwise to expect him to return an MVP level for the Brewers at 33 years old.

Glasnow's season was cut short in August by a right elbow injury, one first labeled as tendonitis but later diagnosed as a sprain following a failed attempt at a return. He said in an offseason interview that imaging in late October appeared to show the elbow being fully healed. While he set a new career high in innings last season before going down, that number being just 134 tells the story. Glasnow had Tommy John surgery in 2021 after missing time earlier in his career with shoulder and forearm trouble, flashing consistent brilliance in between. He had been trending in the right direction with his workload since TJS and proved to be a nice fit in Los Angeles, but his latest injury makes expectations tough to pin down entering 2025. Even if the talented 6-foot-8 righty is healthy and cruising, the Dodgers will probably need to limit him at some point given his injury history.

Naylor set career highs in games played, plate appearances, homers, runs and RBI last season. Volume was clearly a factor, but a career-high ISO was also a major contributor. Naylor needed the boost in power since he was unable to maintain the prior season's batted-ball fortune. The power spike could be fleeting for a number of reasons. Above all, Chase Field in Arizona, his new home venue, suppresses lefty power unlike his old digs in Cleveland which amplifies left-handed pop. A low strikeout rate and a projected spot in the middle of the Diamondbacks' order give Naylor a draftable floor, but plan on a modest power decline.

Contact is the name of the game with Donovan, who sits with a 13.7 percent strikeout rate and an even .280 average through 1,491 career plate appearances. His bat is lacking in terms of thump, however, ranking in the bottom half of the league in average exit velocity and hard-hit rate last season. Donovan logged 652 plate appearances in 2024, second on the team to Paul Goldschmidt, but he managed just 14 homers and five steals, providing fantasy managers with little category juice. He's more than a slap hitter, but Donovan's value is heavily dependent on volume, more so than other hitters in his range. Similar volume is projected in 2025, and eligibility at second base and outfield gives Donovan unique and valuable flexibility.

Bohm's name has been bandied about in trade rumors this winter ahead of his second year of arbitration eligibility. The Phillies are said to be eyeing a roster shakeup of sorts, but so far no team has met Philadelphia's asking price for the third baseman. Bohm had some tough times early in his big-league career, but he's been on the upswing since his infamous "I hate this place" incident in 2022, making his first All-Star team this past season. He hit five fewer homers than he did in 2023, totaling just 15 despite similar batted-ball numbers, following league-wide trends. Bohm has grounded into 41 double plays over the past two seasons which shows his below-average running ability, but at this point he's established as a dependable source of batting average and run production.

Lowe appeared in only 106 games last season as a hamstring issue delayed his debut until early May, and then he was subsequently sidelined with an oblique injury. Lowe appeared overly aggressive at times, swinging at pitches outside the strike zone, and yet he was too passive in the zone, resulting in a high 31.8 percent strikeout rate. If Lowe can improve his approach, he can take advantage of barrel and hard-hit rates in the 70th percentile, along with a 94 percent career success rate on stolen bases (61-for-65). Roster the steals, and hope for better swing decisions in 2025.

Bogaerts started slowly last season, batting .219/.265/.316 over 47 games, perhaps due to learning a new position after an unexpected shift from shortstop to second base. He then suffered a nasty shoulder injury in May, costing him almost two months. After returning, Bogaerts settled in and hit .299/.338/.432 the rest of the way, in line with his 2023 production. His power never developed as hoped and now it's on the decline with three straight seasons of a falling barrel rate. However, Bogaerts has taken advantage of the rules aiding stolen bases, swiping 32 bases in 37 attempts over the past two years. His bat-to-ball skills are still solid, propping up his floor, but there isn't much upside in power or speed. Dual eligibility adds to Bogaerts' appeal, especially in daily leagues.

Rodon got off to a fantastic start in 2024, going 9-2 with a 2.92 ERA and 1.05 WHIP across his first 80 innings (14 starts). He hit some bumps in the road during the summer months, and his season ended on a sour note with three home runs allowed over 3.1 innings in his lone World Series appearance against the Dodgers. Regardless, his 2024 campaign goes down as a considerable success after back, forearm and hamstring injuries cost him half of the previous year and sapped his effectiveness in his first season with the Yankees. His innings totals and performance have been all over the map throughout his career and he's now 32 years old, but recent history bodes rather favorably since Rodon has provided quality numbers across 30-plus starts in two of the past three years. He tentatively lines up as the Yankees' No. 3 starter entering 2025.

An All-Star in 2021 and 2022, Cronenworth fractured his right wrist in August of 2023 which brought to an end to a disappointing campaign. He appeared headed for a rebound season in 2024, posting a .753 OPS in the first half before dipping back to .650 after the break. It would be incorrect to label him a slap hitter, but Cronenworth's slugging percentage has fallen below .400 each of the last three years. He may be best suited as a true utility man, but there is little on the Padres' roster standing in his way of reaching 600 plate yet again. Best of all for fantasy purposes, Cronenworth retains eligibility at first base and second base entering his age-31 season, giving him unique and valuable flexibility, especially in leagues with corner and middle spots.

Abreu is the only reliever in baseball to have struck out 100 or more batters out of the bullpen in each of the past two seasons, joining teammate Josh Hader as well as Fernando Cruz and Mason Miller in that club for 2024. Abreu could challenge for saves on most other clubs, but as long as he and Hader are teammates, Abreu appears to be the Robin to Hader's Batman. Abreu has the highest strikeout rate among all non-closing relievers over the past three seasons, and those strikeouts and stellar ratios make Abreu an interesting play in deep formats. The risk comes in the fact that so few relievers ever work 70-plus innings over consecutive seasons let alone three as Abreu will likely be asked to do with Houston dealing Ryan Pressly away this winter.

Erceg earned his first three career saves with the A's last year and added 14 more with the Royals following a deadline trade, including three during the postseason. He reached a whole new level after the move to Kansas City, pitching to a 2.88 ERA, 0.84 WHIP and 31:3 K:BB across his final 25 regular-season innings. Overall, Erceg threw 67.2 frames around a brief stint on the injured list with forearm tightness. The control he displayed was shocking given his walk rates had consistently been above five per nine since he made the transition from third base to the pitching mound in 2021. While he's been traded twice in recent years and lacks any track record of success beyond last season, Erceg has the high-end fastball velocity and swing-and-miss secondaries to maintain the closer role throughout 2025, if he can keep the walks in check.

Strictly in terms of shutting the door and securing wins for his team, Finnegan has been one of the top closers in baseball over the past couple years. In fact, only Emmanuel Clase, Josh Hader and Raisel Iglesias have more saves than Finnegan since the start of the 2023 season. However, he lacks the swing-and-miss dominance typically associated with the late innings. The Nationals declined to tender Finnegan a contract for 2025 despite his success, making him a free agent in November. Finnegan reined in the long ball and did not allow a single homer over the final two months of last season, but it seems more likely than not that he's without a closer job to begin 2025 since the underlying numbers are not closer-worthy. His experience and success in the ninth should keep him on your radar, but at best he's a speculative endgame pick until there's clarity on his situation.

After serving in a swingman capacity for a couple of years, Martinez is slated to be a full-time starter in 2025. Last season, Martinez started 16 times with 26 relief appearances. His numbers as a reliever were better than as a starter (1.86 ERA relief vs. a 3.84 in the rotation), so he'll be challenged to repeat last year's 3.10 ERA and 1.03 WHIP working out of the Reds' rotation, especially with a below average strikeout rate. Martinez has a starter's arsenal, featuring a four-seam fastball, cutter, sinker and changeup with the occasional curve and slider. Last season's success was driven by a stingy 3.2% walk rate, which he'll be hard-pressed to repeat. Historically, Martinez has been a groundball pitcher, but last season he allowed more flyballs than grounders, though he yielded only 13 homers in 142 1/3 innings. Especially at home, Martinez's success will revolve around his ability to keep the ball in the yard. It's tempting to trust last season's breakthrough, but the paucity of punchouts and likely homer regression tempers expectations.

Wells began 2024 in a timeshare, then emerged as the Yankees' primary backstop. He does not light up his Statcast page, sporting average batted ball skills, but they often improve with young catchers. Wells' high flyball rate supports a solid power floor, but his platoon splits suggest sitting versus southpaws as all 13 of his homers came against right-handers. Strong defense and framing offer leeway to stay in the lineup and improve against southpaws, especially since there is little competition behind the plate in the Bronx after the trade of Jose Trevino to the Reds. Wells' solid plate skills generate a draftable floor, and there are several paths for more production, hence fantasy upside.

Morel was batting just .199/.302/.373 when the Cubs dealt him to the Rays just before the trade deadline. He performed even worse in the junior circuit, posting a .191/.258/.289 line with Tampa Bay. Morel still managed his second 20-homer season while demonstrating progress with more walks and fewer strikeouts. Morel's poor defense will be hidden in left field, where he's ticketed to play regularly. There's potential for 30 homers if he reverts to his pull-heavy approach from 2023, and eligibility at second base and third base -- with bonus outfield eligibility in leagues with a 10-game minimum -- helps soften the blow of the low average.

One of the game's most fun, dynamic young talents, De La Cruz burst forth with a historic, breakthrough 2024 that probably didn't even garner the level of attention it deserved. He managed only the seventh season of at least 25 home runs and 60 stolen bases in history, while becoming only the eight different shortstop ever to play at least 160 games at the position while delivering at least 70 extra-base hits. Sure, De La Cruz struck out a ton (an MLB-leading 218 times), as scouts hinted he might, but his excellent raw metrics (contact quality, bat speed, sprint speed) and 23 years of age suggest he has room to grow all-around. It's easy to formulate a first-round case for him in rotisserie leagues, and points-league managers should keep in mind that he finished 47th overall in scoring despite all those K's.

In this era with a dwindling number of aces, Wheeler is a relative rarity. He and teammate Aaron Nola are the only pitchers to have made at least 30 starts and totaled 190-plus IP as many as four times over the past six seasons. Since the beginning of 2019, Wheeler's 2,413 fantasy points rank second, his 108 quality starts first, his 1,024 2/3 innings rank second, his 1,094 strikeouts third, his 3.14 ERA ninth and his 1.07 WHIP 10th. He also set personal bests as a 34-year-old in 2024 with his 2.57 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, .191 BAA and 26 quality starts, further signaling his skill set rating as one of the most stable at the position. Wheeler is a pitcher around whom you build your fantasy team.

Ragans' follow-up to his astonishing, late-2023 breakthrough went about as well as could possibly have been expected. He maintained almost every statistical gain across his by-far professional bests of 32 starts and 186 1/3 IP, with the only knock on his skills being his losing a tick on his average fastball velocity. Throwing 95.4 mph, however, makes him no slouch in terms of raw stuff, and pitching half of his games in one of the most pitcher-friendly environments helps bolster his case to be a true staff ace. Ragans should be drafted among the top 10 at his position, regardless of format.

Acuna's seven-year MLB career has been quite the rollercoaster ride. He has won NL Rookie of the Year (2018) and MVP Awards (2023). He's had a 41/37 campaign (2019) and the majors' first-ever 40/70 season (2023) on his résumé, yet has also dealt with three separate ACL injuries (among other ailments) including surgeries on both of his knees (the right in 2021, the left in 2024). Fantasy managers should heed Acuna's performance initially returning from surgery the last time, as he missed the first three weeks of 2022 while recovering, then finished 65th on the Player Rater and tied for 175th in fantasy points scored. A sluggish start could be his downside -- tuck that away as a strategic nugget to perhaps instead trade for him in-season -- but his upside remains that of a five-category rotisserie superstar. If reports on his health during spring training look good, he shouldn't slide much further than the first couple of rounds of rotisserie drafts, nor far outside the top-25 overall in points leagues.

Ozuna has been on an amazing two-year run since nearly playing his way out of Atlanta with consecutive terrible seasons in 2021 and 2022. He served exclusively as a designated hitter and in fact started all 162 games at DH last season, returning to elite-level run production once again after it once looked as if 2017 was going to be his peak. Ozuna has driven in 100 runs in each of the past two seasons, and it was all the more impressive in 2024 considering the amount of injuries to the Atlanta lineup over the course of the season. The counting stats seem ultra stable, though his batting average has ranged from .213 to .338 over the past five seasons despite relatively stable walk and strikeout rates, which is a reminder of how is still left up to the randomness of the machinations of baseball. Ozuna may never score 100 runs, but there is little reason to suspect he cannot continue to this current run of success.

A popular pick for AL Rookie of the Year honors entering last season, Caminero's ascent to Tampa Bay was instead delayed by a pair of IL trips due to quadriceps injuries while in Triple-A. He finally got his MLB chance in August, delivering what would have been better-than-70th-percentile Statcast Barrel and hard-hit rates with an above-average contact rate that illustrates his massive offensive upside. Caminero should begin 2025 promised the Rays' everyday 3B role, as well as a heart-of-the-order lineup position. A significant step forward should be well within his reach. He's a potential top-10 positional fantasy option, regardless of format.

Greene was in the midst of a breakthrough 2024, posting nine wins, 13 quality starts, a 2.83 ERA, a 1.02 WHIP and 162 strikeouts through his first 24 starts, before right elbow soreness derailed the rest of his season. He did return in time to make two solid appearances in late September, but the absence added to what has been an alarming injury history in his young MLB career, including IL stints at least five weeks in length in each of his three seasons. Greene has long possessed front-of-the-rotation stuff and, with better luck in the health department, he might yet realize that status in 2025. He's a prospective top-30 fantasy starter with upside, well worth a pick in the middle rounds of your draft.

Westburg earned an All-Star selection in his age-25 season and showed that he should not get lost in the shuffle among the rest of the Orioles' talented young core. His season was interrupted by a fractured right hand, the result of a hit-by-pitch, which cost him most of the final two months. Before going down, Westburg posted an .815 OPS, 18 homers and six steals in 101 games. After serving as the Opening Day designated hitter, Westburg moved around the infield, securing eligibility at second base and third base again entering 2025. Baltimore announced in November that it will be modifying the left-field wall at Camden Yards, moving it in to find a "happier medium," per GM Mike Elias, after the club pushed the wall back prior to 2022. That bodes well for the right-handed-hitting Westburg, who projects to remain a lineup regular.

The 2024 season was a disaster for Strider and his fantasy managers, as the No. 1 pitcher off most draft boards lasted just two starts before succumbing to season-ending elbow surgery -- though he had an internal brace procedure this time after having Tommy John surgery previously in 2019. That gives the right-hander hope of returning in the early stages of 2025. Stiil, there is always risk of setbacks or diminished performance in pitchers initially returning from such a significant operation. When healthy, Strider has been the game's best strikeout artist -- his 458 K's across his span of 54 healthy starts from May 2022-April 2024 were 51 more than the next-closest hurler -- so he'll naturally slide in as one of this year's top risk/reward pitcher picks. Monitor his rehabilitation throughout spring training, as his prognosis could drive his draft value as high as a top-25 SP pick or more of a late-round flier.

Who'd have thought that the same Astros pitcher who surrendered nine runs without escaping the first inning of an April 2024 start would go on to score the 10th-most fantasy points among pitchers across the season's final five months? The introduction of a sinker in May played a big part in that, giving Brown a pitch to minimize hard contact to go along with his 96-mph fastball and whiff-generating knuckle curve. With his more balanced repertoire, he's now capable of top-25 fantasy SP numbers on the high end of his valuation curve. Brown is well worth a mid-round selection in all formats.

Hoffman broke through in a big way in 2023 while pitching in middle relief for the Phillies. Last season, he upped the ante even further by slashing another 3% off his walk rate. Between that and his sharing of the closer duties with Jose Alvarado, Carlos Estevez and Matt Strahm, Hoffman managed a top-20 season, both in rotisserie and points-based scoring. Now with the Blue Jays, Hoffman should take over full-time closer duties, a role from which he could take yet another step forward into the upper tier at his position. Draft him accordingly.

Steer experienced a down year in 2024, though his skills weren't far off from the previous more productive season. He was victimized by the baseball not carrying as well. Steer's flyball exit velocity was nearly the same as 2023, but the average distance dropped seven feet, costing him homers and BABIP. Furthermore, his batting average dropped 46 points, but his expected average fell only 17 points. Steer made up for the loss in power with 25 steals in 28 attempts (89% success rate). New Reds' manager Terry Francona gives the green light to players with a high success rate, so Steer should continue to be a quiet source of steals, with a good chance of a power rebound. He's only missed 10 games over the last two seasons, helping accumulate plentiful runs and RBI. Steer is slated to handle left field but could see action at the corner infield spots.

A top prospect in his earlier seasons as a pro, Ramos' star sagged slightly before he burst onto the scene for the Giants with 20 homers across the final four months of 2024. His mastery of Triple-A ball across the prior year-plus earned him regular at-bats following Michael Conforto's injury in May, and Ramos flashed elite raw power metrics and well above-average speed. That did come with a wide platoon split (198 points of wOBA), a potential advantage to tuck away in ESPN's daily-transactions standard, but Ramos did show enough success against right-handers in the minors that he should take a step forward in 2025. Consider him to be a mid-to-late round pick in larger mixed leagues.

Gurriel had another productive if unspectacular season at the plate for the Diamondbacks in 2024. He contributes to all five categories, but his batting average is arguably his best contribution to a fantasy team's bottom line. Gurriel has been one of the better contact hitters in baseball in recent seasons, but his aversion to walks limits his ability to reach base. His walk and chase rates were both in the bottom 25th percentile last season and do not show any signs of improvement in the near future. The outfielder is at his best when he is facing southpaws, as he has hit .317/.366/.485 against them over the past two seasons compared to .250/.294/.434 against righties.  The retooled lineup in Arizona could have Gurriel hitting cleanup this season which would allow him to potentially drive in 85 runs for the first time in his career. However, some of the leading indicators around his quality of contact trended in a concerning direction in 2024.

Winn drew criticism from fans and fellow players when he threw 100 mph across the diamond in the 2022 Futures Game, but he's no mere gimmick at the shortstop position. Indeed it is thanks largely to his throwing arm and defense that has he has been able to establish himself as an everyday player in St. Louis. Winn also showed impressive growth at the plate last season, posting 15 homers, 11 steals and a .730 OPS across 637 plate appearances at 22 years old after struggling mightily in his first exposure to major-league pitching in 2023. The batted-ball profile does little to excite, but Winn's speed and contact abilities pushed him into the leadoff spot under manager Oliver Marmol and Winn remained there through the end of last season. Winn said over the winter that he is aiming to steal 30-to-40 bases in 2025, which should be taken with a huge grain of salt, but it's nice to know the intent is there.

Moreno is making good on his prospect promise, though injuries limited him to just 97 games last season. At 24 years old, Moreno improved his strikeout and walk rates, showcasing a highly advanced plate approach. He still lost nearly 20 points of batting average, and the catcher finished with a mere five home runs in 351 plate appearances. With a career groundball rate over 50 percent, Moreno's power upside would seem capped, though one can't help but wonder if there is potential for more since he's such a talented hitter. Perhaps the strongest selling point here is his defense, which earned him a Gold Glove in 2023 and should keep him in the primary role behind the plate in Arizona. Beware that there could be another manager lurking in the weeds waiting to draft Moreno at the end in one-catcher leagues.

Garcia played in 157 games last year, but he holds the dubious distinction of his 69 wRC+ being the lowest among all qualified hitters. Fortunately, he swiped 37 bags, the seventh most in MLB. His game is putting the ball in play, mostly on the ground. His Hard-Hit rate and average exit velocity are above average, but not stout enough to supply much pop in power-suppressing Kauffman Stadium. Garcia is not a patient batter, so his time at or near the top of the order are likely over, especially with Jonathan India and a healthy Vinnie Pasquantino in tow. Even though Garcia's skills and defense are best suited for a utility role, he's slated to man the hot corner again in 2025. Even so, relying on Garcia for steals is a slippery slope, since someone else, such as Cavan Biggio, could cut into Garcia's playing time. Having dual second and third base eligibility sweetens Garcia's charm as a streamer in daily formats.

Burleson is coming off a breakout season with the Cardinals in which he hit 21 homers with a team-leading 78 RBI. After making a lone, solitary start against a lefty pitcher in 2023, Burleson made 26 starts against left-handed pitching last season, though he managed just a .514 OPS and three of his 21 homers in 142 total plate appearances against southpaws. With that, he is a candidate for a reduction in playing time, and either way the steals are likely unsustainable given his limited sprint speed. Still, Burleson should be able to do enough damage with the platoon edge to be a worthwhile fourth or fifth outfielder in fantasy, especially if he continues to see most of his time in the two hole for St. Louis. The 26-year-old qualifies at first base in addition to outfield in leagues with a 15-game minimum for eligibility.

Severino and the rest of the Athletics will be playing their home games at Sutter Health Park in West Sacramento this season, in a park that will also remain home to the Triple-A Sacramento River Cats of the Pacific Coast League. The move does not bode well for the pitching staff, at least not on paper, but this is what Severino signed up for when he inked a three-year deal in December. The right-hander rebounded with the Mets in 2024, clearing 30 starts for the first time since 2018 as one of nine pitchers in the National League to exceed 180 innings last season. Severino still throws hard for a starting pitcher, but his strikeout rate has fallen precipitously in recent years, from above 35 percent at his peak to just 21.1 percent last season. The team context and questionable upside will drive many away.

Alcantara, the Cy Young Award winner in the National League in 2022, missed all of last season after undergoing Tommy John surgery in October of 2023. He advanced from regular side sessions to throwing live batting practice last September and will be nearly 18 months removed from the procedure by the time Opening Day rolls around. The Marlins have not publicly disclosed an innings target for Alcantara in 2025, but somewhere around 150 frames likes a good starting point, with room for more if his arm holds up. The injury concerns are not going away anytime soon with a pitcher that throws so hard, but if he proves healthy after the long layoff, Alcantara could prove to be a bargain for fantasy managers at his average draft position. Expect the acquisition cost to rise considerably if Alcantara is pumping gas and looking healthy in spring training.

Pena now has three full major-league seasons under his belt. He has hit 20 homers in a season and he has also stolen 20 bases in a season, but the shortstop has been unable to accomplish both feats in the same campaign. Pena has the pull tendencies one would like to see from someone playing in Houston and hitting from the right side, but his high groundball rate limits his home-run power. Pena has improved his strikeout rate each season he has been in the majors, but he has not shown any willingness to accepts walks. Pena has also stolen double-digit bases each season, but his success rate has been below league average since the rule adjustments two seasons ago. His impatience puts him in the bottom half of the lineup which limits his overall upside, and it's a shame because Pena's numbers could be much better if he were setting the table ahead of the thunder in the lineup.

Pressly signed a two-year deal with the Astros in April of 2022 with a vesting option for 2025, which included a full no-trade clause. After much speculation, Pressly waived that no-trade clause in January to facilitate a move to the Cubs, for whom he's expected to close in 2025. His fantasy outlook is significantly brighter now after Pressly took a back seat to Josh Hader throughout 2024. Pressly is coming off a season in which his fastball continued its decline, putting even more pressure on the right-hander to effectively execute his breaking pitches. This past season saw Pressly's strikeout rate fall below 25 percent for the first time since 2017, and he will likely face competition for saves eventually from Porter Hodge and others in the Chicago bullpen.

Keller took a significant step forward in 2023, setting career highs across the board, and the Pirates rewarded him with a five-year contract extension prior to last season. He then went onto post similar if slightly disappointing numbers in 2024, as his strikeout rate declined four percentage points and both his ERA and WHIP worsened a bit from the previous season. Keller's average fastball velocity dropped about one mile per hour, and every little bit counts when it comes to velocity. His four-seamer saw the most damage of the fastballs as the league hit 80 points better against that pitch. The right-hander is one of just 13 pitchers to throw at least 175 innings each of the past two seasons and Pittsburgh will be leaning on him to stabilize a young rotation in 2025.

Suarez began the 2024 season by going 9-0 with a minuscule 1.36 ERA and 0.79 WHIP across his first 66 innings, only to slide to 3-8 with a 5.10 ERA and 1.52 WHIP over his subsequent 17 starts. The left-hander was said to be dealing with back tightness around the All-Star break and he eventually landed on the injured list as a result of the injury. Despite the way his season trended, it still has to be considered a highly successful campaign, one that further established Suarez as a quality mid-rotation starter in MLB. He is not the most dominant arm in terms of strikeouts, but Suarez keeps the ball on the ground and has one of the National League's best offenses to power him to wins. It's also not crazy to hold out hope that Suarez may still be able to add to his workload in his age-29 season after making the transition from the bullpen a few years ago.

It has been a whirlwind past two years for Skenes.
