His LSU Tigers won the 2023 College World Series behind his performance that earned him its Most Outstanding Player Award and he won the Dick Howser Trophy as college baseball's best player. Skenes was then selected No. 1 overall in that July's amateur draft, ultimately reaching the majors with the Pirates just 10 months later. He'd toss six hitless, 11-strikeout frames in only his second start, kicking off a historic campaign that ultimately earned him NL Rookie of the Year honors. Skenes' electric raw stuff (a 99-mph average fastball, slider and splinker) grades among the best in the majors already despite his youth, and he's already drawing favorite's odds for the 2025 Cy Young Award -- a testament to his overwhelming upside. If there's any reason to hesitate in building your fantasy team around him, it's that the Pirates have been cautious with his workload, coupled with the typical worries we have with young pitchers throwing large IP totals. But hey, isn't every pitcher an injury risk to some degree?

When the curtain closes on Harper's career, he's going to go down as one of the all-time greats, even if during its course it felt like he sometimes fell shy of expectations. Across just the past 10 seasons, Harper has five seasons of 30-plus homers, six of at least a .280 batting average, and five with at least a .900 OPS. The only other player who can make that same claim during that time span is Mike Trout. Now 32, Harper continues to possess elite contact and a patient approach, meaning he should have a few more solid fantasy seasons ahead of him. That he bats in the heart of a still-productive Phillies lineup, in their homer-friendly venue, certainly helps his early-round valuation.

Injuries once again hampered Seager, who has now spent time on the IL in five of his past seven seasons, resulting in a combined 333 regular-season games missed over that stretch. A hip issue cut his 2024 short in early September, and hernia surgeries bookended his season (one in January, one in September). Nevertheless, Seager remained healthy enough to hit 30-plus homers for the third consecutive season and, at the time he got hurt, he had the sixth-most fantasy points among shortstops and 25th-most of all hitters. His underlying metrics, too, were as good as they have been at any point during the past five seasons, signaling that he's still every bit the early-round pick.

One of baseball's most consistent power sources, but also one of its most free-swinging hitters, Hernandez has hit 25-plus homers in each of the last five full MLB seasons and 32-plus in two of his last four. By returning to the Dodgers this winter, he chose to remain in one of the game's better home run environments, as well as one of its most potent lineups. Hernandez should again deliver value akin to his 2024, which had him a top-25 rotisserie and top-75 overall points league performer.

Imanaga got off to a historic start with the Cubs last season, posting a 0.84 ERA across his first 53.2 innings, the lowest mark ever through a pitcher's first nine MLB starts. The lefty earned an All-Star selection in his first season stateside and finished third in the National League with 15 wins, while only George Kirby and Tarik Skubal ranked higher among qualified starters in terms of strikeout-to-walk ratio. Home runs were a problem on occasion -- Imanaga allowed multiple homers seven times -- and those concerns will follow him into 2025, as fantasy managers may hold their breath in tough matchups. The Cubs are working with him on that issue, and overall his stuff translated quite well as he made the jump from Nippon Professional Baseball at 30 years old. Expect some giveback, but Imanaga looks like a legitimate frontline starter, one probably best viewed as an SP2 for fantasy purposes.

Don't regard Santander's career-best, 44-HR explosion as a sign of his growing power, because his underlying metrics were almost spot-on to his 2022-23 rates, with Statcast's expected home runs having him pegged for only slightly more than he hit in either of those two years (36.6, versus 33.3 in 2022 and 2023). Santander's appeal in fantasy leagues is his consistency, as he has hit .244 while averaging 95 RBI, 83 runs scored and 153 games played across the past three seasons, never deviating by more than 13 points of batting average, seven RBI, eight runs or two games in any individual year. He's the epitome of the "very good, though not elite" outfielder, but that's still a fine early-round pick in any format.

The Cardinals announced in November that Contreras will be a full-time first baseman and designated hitter moving forward. It brings to an end a rather strange saga in which the team soured on his catching abilities shortly after signing him, moving him out from behind the plate for a stretch previously in 2023. Contreras fractured his forearm on a catcher's interference in May of last year when he was struck by a J.D. Martinez swing, and he broke a finger on a HBP later in the season. He still managed 15 home runs in just 84 games, and Contreras has been above league average at the plate in every single season of his career. Now 34 and overshadowed by his younger brother, Contreras will potentially get lost in the shuffle at first base when he loses catcher eligibility in 2026, but he should still be treated as a premium option at the catcher position for 2025.

The Yankees' big hitting acquisition following Juan Soto's free-agent departure, Bellinger brings his pull-power, fly ball-oriented swing to Yankee Stadium -- possibly the best fit yet for his skill set. Though Bellinger's contact-quality metrics have been below-average for four years running, he gets the most out of his swings, and his improved contact over the last two seasons gives him as much of a chance at contributing batting average as well as home runs. A rebound to his 2023 norms might be a stretch, but it's not entirely out of the question in pinstripes. He's well worth a mid-round selection.

Sanchez impressed by going 11-9 with a 3.32 ERA and 1.24 WHIP across 181.2 innings last season, his first as a full-time member of the Philadelphia rotation. The lefty's game is built around the sinking fastball which was the main driver in a 57.4 percent groundball rate last season, third highest among qualified starters. In turn, he allowed just 11 homers for the third-best HR/9 among that group. Sanchez can also pull the string on a changeup and spin a breaking ball, though the package has not included many strikeouts to date. It's possible that Sanchez, still just 28 years old, could unlock another level with the strikeouts, but that should not be expected since there is little reason to mess with a formula that has been largely successful. The K rate as it stands now caps his upside, but Sanchez looks like a viable pick to fill out any fantasy rotation in 2025.

The aging curve appears to have taken hold with Goldschmidt, as his age-37 season saw him post his worst strikeout, walk and home run rates and the lowest isolated power and batting averages of his 14-year MLB career. He did, however, hit 20 home runs across his final 117 games, while mashing lefties (.295/.366/.473), and the move from Busch Stadium to Yankee Stadium should only help him in terms of park factors. Goldschmidt might have one more top-10 fantasy 1B season left in his bat, though his recent trend makes him a wiser player to target for your mixed-league corner infield position.

His first taste of the majors was just 21 months after he was selected No. 1 overall in the 2022 amateur draft, but Holliday flopped in what became only a 10-game audition for the Orioles (.059 BA, 18 K's in 34 AB). . He was returned to Triple-A ball and rendered a relative afterthought for the next three months. But, as is often the case with blue-chip prospects, he returned to homer in five of his next 10 games while posting top-shelf raw speed metrics and what would have been a 73rd percentile hard hit rate if he had the requisite at-bats to qualify. Holliday's skills still point to him being a future fantasy superstar and, as a 21-year-old, he remains a dynasty building block. He's projected to be the team's starting second baseman in 2025. With a strong spring, he'll be a high upside mid-to-late rounder -- even in redraft formats.

Not often are 26-year-olds asked to front pitching rotations, but that is where Gore finds himself with Washington entering the 2025 season. Gore has made 59 starts for the Nationals since arriving from San Diego as part of the Juan Soto deal, and he made good strides in his second season with the organization. Gore increased his workload by 30 innings while reducing his HR/9 from 1.8 to 0.8, throwing with more velocity and posting a sub-4.00 ERA for the first time in his career. He got to double-digit wins, but the 3.90 ERA and 1.42 WHIP do not go together, with the latter implying Gore was fortunate when it came to run prevention. It's reasonable to be picking up Mitch Keller vibes here because the similarities in their career paths are a bit uncanny. Whether or not Gore can shoulder a 180-plus-inning workload is the lingering question.

Through three injury-riddled seasons, Lodolo's ERA is 4.52, but his xFIP is 3.74 with a 3.53 SIERA. After posting a 29% strikeout rate over his first two seasons, it fell to 24.7% last season, but Lodolo was dealing with lingering effects from a stress reaction in his left tibia, a groin strain and finger issues. His velocity was up from 2023, but he didn't generate as many swinging strikes from his curve and changeup, while increasing sinker usage, which is designed to induce groundballs and not swing and misses. Still just 27 years old, if Lodolo can shake the injury bug, he can become the pitcher teased by his ERA estimators. The risk is worth the reward to hope he finally realizes his potential.

Mullins has faded into the background a bit over the past few years as young stars like Gunnar Henderson and Adley Rutschman have emerged in Baltimore, but the speedy outfielder continues to produce useful numbers for fantasy managers. Chances are, Mullins will never hit 30 home runs again like he did during his breakout 2021 campaign, but Mullins has launched at least 15 homers each of the past three seasons, providing enough power to complement his speed and keep him viable in mixed leagues. A batting average in the .230s has hurt over the past two seasons, and his playing time against lefties only continues to trend downward, but Mullins' floor against right-handed pitching looks fairly sturdy. He will make over $8 million in his final year of arbitration eligibility.

Abreu's impressive minor-league performances in 2022 and 203 got him on some radars, and his first full season of big-league play had its moments. Abreu didn't steal bases like he did in 2022 when he stole 31 bags in Double-A nor did he reach base at a .390 clip as he did between Triple-A and the majors in 2023, but Abreu was a monster against righties, slashing .266/.334/.491 with 14 of his 15 homers. His production against righties was 26 percent above league average, but that all changed against southpaws. His struggles against left-handed pitching are why the likes of Rob Refsnyder persists on the Boston depth chart as the duo make a solid tandem while the club tries to figure out whether Abreu can handle lefties or is destined for a strong-side platoon future like many lefties before him.

Boyd fared remarkably well in his return from June 2023 Tommy John surgery across eight late-season starts and an additional three during the postseason, posting a 2.28 ERA and a 28.2% strikeout rate. Most importantly, both his slider and changeup appeared to have similar life to their pre-surgery models, which was apparently enough for the Cubs to commit $29 million to him across the next two seasons. Boyd's career has reflected much streakiness in terms of his control, and his injury history is a concern. However, so long as he's valued as more of a back-of-your-staff mixed-league type, he's well worth taking a chance.

Ward established new career highs in plate appearances (663), hits (144) and home runs (25) last season, leading the Angels in all three categories. He still has not been able to replicate the full extent of his success from 2022 when he slashed .281/.360/.473 over 564 plate appearances, but Ward's 2024 season represented a bright spot for the organization as well as an impressive personal rebound. Remember, his 2023 campaign was cut short when he suffered multiple facial fractures on a hit-by-pitch and there are often mental hurdles that accompany such an injury. Ward's strikeout rate ticked up to close to 25 percent last season, but he was still an above-average offensive contributor, and as he enters his age-31 season, he appears set to continue anchoring the heart of the order for Anaheim.

The Mets have given Soto's fantasy managers 765 million reasons to trust in his elite talent. He's one of six players in history to register a .400 OBP in each of his first seven seasons, and one of three from that group (Ted Williams, Frank Thomas) to also manage at least a 140 OPS-plus in each year. Soto's 201 career home runs before turning 26 are also tied for sixth-most in history, and he's the only player to register a top-15 fantasy point total among hitters in each of the past six seasons. He is the epitome of the high-floor, safe return on investment first-round pick, even if his profit potential is greater in leagues that reward his patience. Nevertheless, Soto could be headed for a prime-years uptick, playing the 2025 season at the age of 26.

Only a left ankle sprain which cost him three weeks in late August/early September stood in Marte's way towards cementing his status as one of fantasy baseball's most productive hitters, but perhaps that missed time (and how it influences the perception of his worth) will merely serve to keep him affordable come draft day. He set personal bests with his 36 home runs and 95 RBI, fully supported by huge spikes in contact quality. His hard-hit rate was 14% greater than his career number in the category and he made huge strides defensively at second base. For you daily-transactions folks, bear in mind that his .414 wOBA against left-handed pitchers over the past five seasons is third-best in baseball (minimum 150 plate appearances). Consider taking Marte, a top-25 performer in both fantasy points and on our Player Rater last year, in the opening rounds of any draft.

A model of consistency for more than a decade, Freeman has scored 400-plus fantasy points in eight of his 14 full MLB seasons, matching Mike Trout for the most by any player during that time span, while finishing among the top-25 overall on the Player Rater in five of the past seven years. Freeman's combination of polished approach at the plate and elite quality of contact makes him one of the highest-floor players in fantasy baseball, even as his age-35 season dawns. Sure, his so-so second half -- his .790 OPS after the All-Star break was his worst in any half-season since 2015's second half -- beckons questions about the aging curve, and the ankle injury that bothered him late in the year (and in the postseason) which required December surgery warrants a spring check-in. That said, Freeman is otherwise a rock-solid, foundational piece to select in your draft's opening rounds.

Sale's Comeback Player of the Year campaign earned him his first career Cy Young Award in 2024, fueled by what were his best single-year strikeout, whiff and hard-hit rates allowed as well as his best average fastball velocity since before his March 2020 Tommy John surgery. Best yet, he only seemed to improve as the season progressed, posting a 1.88 ERA and a 33.2% strikeout rate across his final 16 starts, signaling his ability to maintain an elite level of performance despite his 35 years of age. Back issues prematurely ended Sale's campaign. That's an injury which bears watching throughout spring training, but if he's in the clear on that front, he's plenty capable of delivering top-10 fantasy SP numbers again.

Bregman's elite plate discipline makes him a valued points-league fantasy player. However, he was only 56th in scoring in 2024, after finishing top-30 in four of the previous six seasons. Maybe his middling contact-quality metrics have begun to catch up with him? A .276/.325/.532, 17-HR performance across his final 62 games offered encouragement that his 2022-24 baselines can be repeated, but the fact remains that he hasn't had a better-than-46th-percentile Statcast Barrel or better-than-51st-percentile hard hit rate since 2018. Where Bregman signs as a free agent will have a say in his fantasy utility -- players with his on-base skills fluctuate more in value based upon who hits behind them and how often their teams' lineups turn over. Until that's known, he's an early-round pick in points leagues and more of a borderline top-100 type in rotisserie.

Few players possess Kwan's elite level of bat control, as evidenced by his 88.9% contact and 28.1% line-drive rates across his three MLB seasons, second- and eighth-best among hitters with at least 900 plate appearances during that time span. At one point in 2024, that put him on a quest for a .400 batting average, before a rise in his launch angle contributed to what was a disappointing, .206 second-half batting average. Kwan's game lacks power, and his raw speed dipped noticeably last season, so he'll need to decide just what kind of hitter he wants to be. As an elite-contact, .300-hitting, 20-SB player with minimal power, he'll remain valuable in any fantasy format, particularly points-based scoring. Consider him in the early rounds in those leagues and slightly later in rotisserie formats.

Smith's wRC+ declined for the fourth straight season, but his 111 mark was still one of the top efforts from a catcher, especially one with the sixth most plate appearances at the position. With Shohei Ohtani joining the Dodgers, Smith only served as the DH three times. However, there is evidence that his drop in production wasn't necessarily due to the extra games behind the plate. April was by far Smith's best month with a .397 wOBA, then the final five months fell between .279 and .332, with September being his second-best month. Since 2021, only Salvador Perez has had more plate appearances as a backstop and just J.T. Realmuto has caught more innings than Smith, so a gentle drop in exit velocity and Hard-Hit rate is understandable. Even so, Smith's quality and quantity of contact remain solid for the position, keeping Smith among the first backstops off the board.

Happ tied a career high with 25 home runs in 2024 and also set career bests in runs (89) and RBI (86), while his .782 OPS remained in line with his marks from the previous two seasons. The veteran outfielder also recorded double-digit steals (13) for the second consecutive campaign, which he didn't accomplish in his first six big-league seasons. He continues to showcase his patience and finished tied-fifth in MLB with 80 walks, and he has a double-digit walk rate in four of the past five years. Happ has also won three straight Gold Gloves in left field for the Cubs, which helps him stick in the lineup through any slumps. He's played in nearly 96 percent of Chicago's games over the past five years and has provided a consistently above-average bat throughout his career, so Happ should be a reliable target for fantasy managers in 2025.

The Cardinals signed Gray to a three-year contract in November of 2023, but GM John Mozeliak made it clear this winter that lowering payroll is a priority heading into the 2025 season. With that, Gray is on the block, though he has a full no-trade clause. He won 13 games last season, his most since 2015, and finished third among qualified starters in strikeout percentage. Gray ended the season in the injured list with right forearm flexor tendonitis, but he was expected to have a normal offseason. Whether he stays in St. Louis or goes is a matter of little concern, since Gray is used to bouncing around the league. Health remains his biggest obstacle. The 35-year-old has averaged just over 150 innings per year over the past four seasons.

Arozarena's stock has fallen in the past calendar year. He got off to a brutal start to 2024 with a .461 OPS through the end of April and the Rays later traded him to the Mariners for a pair of prospects and a player to be named later, in line with their usual modus operandi. The outfielder first broke out in the 2020 playoffs when he hit 10 homers, most in postseason history, and in the years since he's turned in four consecutive 20-20 seasons. However, T-Mobile Park in Seattle was the worst in baseball for offense last season by MLB's own park factors, and the lineup around him is underwhelming. Worst of all for his long-term outlook, Arozarena's defense has been dismal in recent years, wiping out a lot of his value to real-world teams. Eventually, that will cost him playing time and the volume will no longer be there to prop him up.

Flaherty returns to Detroit, where he enjoyed a bounce-back beginning to his 2024, before cooling somewhat after a deadline trade to the Dodgers. Thanks in large part to improved command of his signature slider, his strikeout rate rebounded to near his 2018-19 peak, and he tallied 162 IP, his most in five seasons. Flaherty's 2021-22 injury history might always be a lingering worry, but the improvements he made last season give him good odds of delivering similar numbers this year. He should be selected as a third or fourth fantasy starter in mixed leagues.

Martinez began the season with Triple-A Reno, but after punching out 14 hitters in 6.2 innings, he was called up in mid-April. Early on, he worked in low-leverage scenarios, notching his first hold June 4. Martinez then serves as a setup man until August when he took over as the primary closer for Arizona. He converted eight of nine chances over the final two months and Martinez has stuff to continue closing as he averages triple digits on his four-seam fastball and sinker, though can struggle to locate on occasion. His WHIP will be high with the walks, so saves will come with ratio baggage. Just 23 years old, Martinez can certainly learn to throw more strikes. He'll enter the season as the favorite for saves in the desert, though A.J. Puk looms if Martinez's control issues yield too many blown saves.

While many might regard Torres' career thus far as a disappointment, he has nevertheless carved out a plenty productive role for himself. Over his seven MLB seasons, his 138 home runs rank third-most among second basemen and he's one of only four at the position with at least 100 homers and 50 steals. Torres did benefit from the hitter-friendly home environment of Yankee Stadium, as well as the often potent Yankees lineup, so some regression is to be expected now that he's a member of the Tigers. Still, Torres seems to have settled in as an annual 25-HR, 10-SB, .265-hitting type with top-10 positional fantasy value. Plus, he did finish an underwhelming 2024 on a high note (.297/.369/.453, 7 HR over his final 45 games, playoffs included). Expect similar value from him in 2025.

A prospect's growth isn't always linear and a veteran's decline isn't always gradual. Case in point: Springer. There is a chance Springer enjoys a renaissance season in 2025, but his quality of contact metrics are quickly heading in the wrong direction and they usually don't reverse at 35 years old. Springer's hard-hit rate and average exit velocity were career lows last season. In addition, his groundball rate has increased each of the last three seasons, sapping power. Once a top-of-the-order mainstay, Springer is now best suited for the lower half of the lineup. Solid plate skills keep Springer fantasy relevant, but there is arguably more downside than upside at this stage.

Volpe's sophomore season reflected only minimal growth, mostly in the form of his contact rate. Almost every other underlying metric regressed, with the primary reasons for his improving from SS29 to SS17 (both on the Player Rater and in fantasy points scored) coming from his gains in both runs scored and steals. Volpe will need to either boost his ground-ball rate or his contact quality metrics -- and preferably both -- in order to move much further up the ranks, though the Yankees remain committed to him as their starting shortstop. They might even give him more looks from the leadoff spot, should he continue his contact gains or restore his 2023 level of patience, which would further fill those two important rotisserie departments. Consider him to be a solid mixed-league middle infielder.

Following his return from July 2023 elbow surgery -- an internal brace procedure, after he had twice previously had Tommy John surgery -- Rasmussen was eased back into action by the Rays, largely as a reliever. He acclimated himself well to the switch, reflecting spikes in his average fastball velocity and strikeout rate, which offers promise heading into 2025. Rasmussen should return to the Rays rotation to begin the year, but keep in mind that their conservative approach to pitching workloads means the right-hander might be looking at closer to a 120- than a 160-inning workload. Still, he has the skills to be an every-start fantasy option while available if his stuff looks as good in March as it did last September.

An oblique strain put Muncy on the shelf in May and eventually forced a move to the 60-day injured list since he was slow to progress. He finally made it back in August and was a regular in the lineup throughout the Dodgers' run to the World Series, doing typical Muncy things with a .163 average but also three homers and 15 walks in the postseason. At 34 years old, Muncy is well established as a low-average, high-OBP slugger from the left side. Given the depth in Los Angeles and his splits in recent years, it seems likely that he will remain limited to a platoon, starting primarily against right-handed pitching. That in theory limits his upside, but Muncy's immense power and the lineup around him make him a potential option at third base or corner infield once the everyday players are off the board.

Ohtani has scripted quite the résumé already over his seven MLB seasons: Rookie of the Year (2018), MVP honors (2021), first player in history to hit 30-plus homers while also striking out 200-plus batters (2022), back-to-back MVPs (2023-24) and, most recently, becoming the charter member of baseball's 50/50 club (2024). While further history book rewrites might seem logically unattainable for the now-30-year-old, it's still within the realm of possibility that he'll score a career-high total fantasy points in 2025 and/or set a personal best in Wins Above Replacement. As both a hitter and pitcher from 2021-23 -- his expected role once again in 2025 -- Ohtani averaged 214 fantasy points more than the league's next-best player annually, an advantage that can be readily exploited in ESPN's standard game with its daily transaction format. Ohtani's fantasy utility hinges heavily upon how your league handles him, but a universal, No. 1 overall case is a relatively easy one.

While not a lock, Machado might very well be headed to Cooperstown one day, and he continued to produce at a high level in 2024. The third baseman smacked 29 homers and finished third in the National League with 105 RBI, marking the third time he's cleared the century mark in the last four seasons. Machado's OBP has dipped in recent years as his patience has waned, but he continues to hit the ball hard and remains a model of good health, clearing 600 plate appearances in each of the last nine full MLB seasons. He endured a rough month of May and grounded into 25 double plays last year, most in the majors, which speaks to his reduced mobility at 32 years old. Perhaps he will be a bit more susceptible to streakiness moving forward, but for now, Machado can still be a viewed as a foundational piece of any fantasy offense.

How you regard Burnes might come down to these conflicting thoughts: Is his precipitous, four-year pattern of declining strikeout rates worrisome, or does the Diamondbacks' six-year, $210 million commitment to the right-hander strengthen confidence in his skills? The answer might lie somewhere in between. Burnes and Logan Webb are the only pitchers with at least 95 starts, 60 quality starts and 590 IP over the past three seasons. That durailbity, combined with his repertoire tweaks -- he's increasingly going for minimizing hard contact rather than for swings and misses -- diminish the instinct to panic about possible skills erosion. Burnes might no longer be a Cy Young favorite, but he looks the part of dependable top-10 fantasy starting pitcher.

Albies is a three-time All-Star and two-time Silver Slugger, but injuries have kept him under 100 games played in two of the past three seasons. First, a fractured right toe put him on the shelf last year before a fractured left wrist cost him most of the summer. There was some uncertainty as to whether he would return last season, but Albies made it back for nine games at the very end of the campaign. In addition to the injuries, there have been chirps that Albies could or perhaps should give up switch hitting given his career splits as a left-handed hitter against right-handed pitching (.247/.309/.434). Despite the flaws in his profile, Albies is arguably still right up there among the top second basemen on the board, maybe behind only Ketel Marte. As he enters his age-28 season, Albies will be attempting to turn the page on his recent health woes and return to 30-10 production for Atlanta.

A big, powerful prospect, albeit one with a good amount of swing-and-miss in his game, Wood should make a sizable leap in the home run category in 2025. After hitting 26 homers in 129 minor league games in 2023, then another 10 in 52 games for Triple-A Rochester to begin last season, he arrived in Washington to deliver what would have been 95th-percentile-or-better exit velocity and hard-hit rates. Wood will need to get more lift in his swing to realize his massive home run potential -- his ground-ball rate was 55% as a rookie -- but between that possibility and the above-average speed that has helped him average 18 steals across four professional seasons, he'll be plenty appealing as a breakthrough pick in rotisserie leagues as is. Consider him in the middle rounds.

Yamamoto, one of the most ballyhooed Japanese arrivals of the past decade-plus, had a U.S. debut season that will be regarded by most as a disappointment. From the five runs in just a single inning's work he surrendered in his big-league debut last March, to the near-three months he missed due to a triceps injury, he never got much of an extended chance to showcase his tremendous raw stuff. Yamamoto did, however, enjoy a 12-start stretch with a 2.41 ERA and 28.5% strikeout rate, and his four-seam fastball, splitter and curveball each registered excellent marks. The ingredients of a staff ace -- granted one subject to the six-man rotation and a probable innings cap -- are still here.

Miller's campaign was one of the most underappreciated -- not only in 2024, but across all historical rookie RP seasons. He became only the third rookie reliever to manage at least 25 saves, 100 strikeouts and a sub-2.50 ERA (Terry Forster, 1972; Craig Kimbrel, 2011), and among all pitchers with at least 50 IP in 2024, he led in strikeout rate (41.8%), average fastball velocity (100.9 mph) and Statcast-expected ERA (1.77). Miller, who previously had durability concerns, missed only two weeks' time to injury when he fractured his pinky punching a padded table, and a short-relief role seemed to suit his skill set. He has assumed a place as one of the game's best fantasy relievers, and it's a plus for 2025 that his Athletics made winter moves hinting at more of a push to compete.

Duran is coming off a second consecutive 20-plus-save season, though his role in the Minnesota bullpen has been somewhat in fluid, more so than fantasy managers would like. As a rookie in 2022, he blew batters away with an 18.1 percent swinging-strike rate and an elite strikeout-minus-walk percentage. However, he has not been able to achieve the same level of overall success over the past two seasons. This past year saw a reduction in his strikeout rate while opponents hit 28 points higher against Duran. He also struggled to prevent runners from scoring when they got on base. It feels like a pitcher with this much swing and miss and such a high groundball rate should have better outcomes than what Duran has earned to date. The expected stats show what Duran's is capable of.

Castillo's season ended in early September as a result of a hamstring strain, but he's expected to be 100 percent in the spring. Previously more of an groundball pitcher in Great American Ball Park, he has adjusted to T-Mobile Park, inducing more flyballs. Even in the bigger yard, Castillo's homers have increased, though the corresponding drop in BABIP has lowered his WHIP, so he is no longer a detriment in that category. After two seasons with a strikeout rate over 27 percent, Castillo slid to 24.3 percent last season, coinciding with a drop in swinging-strike rate. His once vaunted changeup lost some of its effectiveness, likely due to his four-seam fastball dropping a couple of ticks. He was once a borderline fantasy ace, but Castillo is now merely solid as he enters his age-32 season.

Garcia's 2024 season was a massive step backward after he was an All-Star in two of the previous three years. His slugging percentage was down more than 100 points from 2023 while his .284 OBP was sixth worst among qualified hitters. Garcia still reached 25 homers and 11 steals, though his offensive struggles combined with poor marks on defense could threaten his playing time in 2025. The Rangers figure to give Garcia every chance to bounce back, but the pressure will be on for the 32-year-old to produce at a high level given his limited defensive utility. Garcia missed the end of last season with a knee injury, but surgery was deemed unnecessary and he is expected to enter spring training without limitations.

After an offseason flooded with trade rumors, Arenado returns to St. Louis for a fifth season. His performance has taken a step backwards in both of the last two campaigns, coinciding with the typical downward aging curve a player set to turn 34 years old in April might follow. Back and forearm injuries in those seasons might have played a part, but Arenado has never seen such poor contact-quality metrics as he did in 2024. He'll need to reverse those to remain a top-10 capable fantasy third baseman, and it's not unheard of that a player of his caliber can squeeze out one more productive year at this stage of his career. It's still wiser to regard Arenado a mid-round, mid-range pick unless he looks great during the exhibition season.

After several years spent toiling in mediocrity between the rotation and bullpen, Lugo enjoyed a surprise breakout at 34 years old in his first season as a member of the Royals' rotation. He was a first-time All-Star and won 16 games, tied for second in the American League. Lugo surged past 200 innings for the first time ever after previously topping out at 146.1 frames in 2023. It's rather tough to buy into given Lugo's lack of strikeouts or track record, but he has one of the best defenses in the majors behind him. The righty had nine different pitches categorized by Statcast last season, and that ability to throw the kitchen sink helps keep opposing hitters off balance and off his four-seam fastball. He may be a fade for some, but it's possible Lugo found something with Kansas City that will allow him to continue beating the estimators in 2025.

O'Hoppe struck out nearly 30 percent of the time last season, but overall he was a bright spot for a last-place Angels squad, hitting 20 homers and providing plus value behind the plate. After missing a large chunk of 2023 with a shoulder injury, O'Hoppe seemed to hit a wall in August of last season, posting a .339 OPS that month before rebounding to .791 in September. Drafted in the 23rd round out of high school in 2018, O'Hoppe has proven to be a tremendous find and developmental success story for the organization. The strikeouts should be manageable with his batted-ball profile, and improvement against left-handed pitching seems likely given his 2023 numbers. Entering his age-25 season, O'Hoppe appears capable of jumping a tier or two at the catcher position while playing his home games at a park that is generally favorable for right-handed power.

Lee suffered a season-ending shoulder injury in May when he crashed into the outfield fence at Oracle Park, necessitating surgery. The expectation is that Lee will be a full go for the start of spring training in 2025 as he enters Year 2 of a six-year contract with the Giants following a storied career with the Kiwoom Heroes of the Korea Baseball Organization. At age 25, Lee debuted in the majors with a .289 batting average across his first 20 games before dipping to .226 across his subsequent 17 games. It was a rather tiny sample in the end, but the contact that he was known for in the KBO translated, with Lee striking out just 13 times across 158 plate appearances. The big question is whether Lee can tap into enough power to be worthwhile in mixed leagues, but that may be tough in San Francisco. It's also possible that Lee could lose out on some at-bats against left-handed pitching.

One of the game's best hit-tool prospects, Wilson posted a .412 batting average and 97% contact rate in his final college season at Grand Canyon, .333/89% numbers in his 26-game pro debut in 2023, and .433/.93% numbers as a minor leaguer in 2024. That earned him a mid-July promotion to the Athletics, where he unfortunately suffered a hamstring injury in his MLB debut that cost him the next five weeks. Wilson returned to record similarly strong contact metrics as the team's starting shortstop down the stretch, and he figures to serve in the same role to begin 2025. He's lacking in much else at this stage of his career, but this is the kind of high-floor player mixed-leaguers should want from their middle infield spot.

Smith emerged from relative obscurity last season to become one of the top arms in the Cleveland bullpen, pitching to a sparkling 1.91 ERA, 0.90 WHIP and 103:17 K:BB over 75.1 innings. Despite notching just one save, Smith outearned many closers in standard scoring, including Kenley Jansen and Jhoan Duran among others. His walk rates on the farm suggest he could give back some of his gains in that particular department, but Smith looks here to stay given that he has three dominant pitches in his four-seamer, splitter and sweeper. At 25 years old, Smith is already a remarkable success story, having signed with the Guardians as an undrafted free agent in 2020. Emmanuel Clase is standing in his way of regular save chances, but Smith looks like closer material in the long term, and in the short term he will be highly coveted in leagues scoring holds.

Buxton exclusively worked at designated hitter throughout 2023 in an attempt to keep him healthy, but he played in just 85 contests before returning to center field for the Twins last season. His return to the outfield was overall a success as his 102 games played represented his largest workload since 2017, but he still battled injuries and has reached 400 plate appearances in a season just once in his big-league career. Buxton took a major step backward at the plate in 2023, but he rebounded last year with 18 home runs and a .279/.335/.524 slash line, with the resurgence being supported by a 48.1 percent hard-hit rate. The 31-year-old has played in just over 57 percent of Minnesota's games across the past three seasons, so 90-100 games is a reasonable estimate for him in 2025. Fantasy managers will obviously be hoping for more than that, especially coming off a clean offseason, but expectations should still be tempered given his lengthy injury history.

Doval tied for the National League lead in saves in 2023 when he racked up 39, but he pitched his way out of the closer role last season and even off the major-league roster for a stretch in August. The right-hander lost his feel for the strike zone, posting the second-highest walk percentage among qualifying relievers at 14.4 percent. Doval wasn't much better in that regard following his return from Triple-A, handing out 10 free passes in his final 13 big-league innings. Ryan Walker took over the ninth inning for the Giants when Doval was demoted and seems likely to have the inside track on the closer job in 2025 given his success down the stretch last season. That doesn't mean Doval can't return to the closer role, as he has electric stuff, but he probably still has some work to do to regain the trust of manager Bob Melvin.

O'Hearn has flourished on the busier side of a platoon, mashing 28 of 30 homers since 2022, and all 15 last season versus right-handers. When he didn't start, O'Hearn usually pinch hit, so he garnered more playing time than a typical lefty platoon batter. Last season, O'Hearn's strikeout rate dropped to a career low 14.0% mark, but his Hard-Hit rate fell precipitously, so he ended up with a 119 wRC+, just a point higher than 2023. There are sexier players with a higher ceiling, but O'Hearn provides a stable floor, embellished by hitting in the middle of a potent lineup. Dual first base and outfield eligibility add to his streaming allure.

A paragon of fantasy baseball excellence across the past nine seasons, Betts has hit .294 while averaging 30 home runs, 88 RBI, 19 stolen bases, 113 runs scored and 503 fantasy points per 162 team games over that time. His cumulative numbers in those categories rank ninth (minimum 2,000 plate appearances), seventh, ninth, ninth, first and second overall. Additionally, he entered both 2024 (OF/2B) and 2025 (OF/SS) with dual-positional eligibility and added additional eligibility in-season in 2023 (2B, SS) and 2024 (SS). Even at 32 years old, Betts appears primed for another year of steady, first round-caliber production, in large part due to his elite plate discipline and positioning atop the productive Dodgers lineup, one of the most fantasy-friendly roles in the league.

Coming off a sizzling finish to 2023 where he scored the most SP fantasy points across his final eight starts, Skubal exploded with a 2024 for the ages, culminating in the AL Cy Young Award. He maintained his 2023 control gains (sixth-ranked 4.6 BB%), added another full tick to his average fastball velocity (third-ranked 96.8 mph), and delivered 20-plus fantasy points in a MLB-leading (tied with Zack Wheeler) 14 of his 31 starts. Best yet, Skubal maintained elite performance across the entire six-month calendar, scoring more points over the Tigers' final 81 regular-season games (279) than in their first 81 (274). It placed him at the forefront of the fantasy SP rankings, though as is true with almost any pitcher these days, he's not completely without risk, with 2017 Tommy John and August 2022 flexor tendon surgeries on his résumé. Hey, sometimes you have to close your eyes tight and roll the dice.

Olson was not exempt from the seemingly team-wide funk that struck the 2024 Braves. He posted his worst OPS and OPS-plus as well as his worst strikeout, walk, home run, hard-hit and Statcast Barrel rates since the abbreviated 2020 campaign, although his cumulative numbers wound up looking eerily similar to his 2022 effort. His 2024 looked unusually unlucky and the fact he finished the year on a .282/.380/.573, 16-HR flourish across the Braves' final 60 games suggests that he'll rebound to a degree. Olson was effectively a top-40 overall player in points leagues and a top-70 rotisserie perforner in 2021-22, which seems like a fair valuation for what to expect from him in 2025.

Crochet didn't merely break out in his first season back in a pitching rotation since his Tennessee days -- his 2024 performance was historic. He became the first pitcher in the modern era to strike out at least 140 batters with 20 walks or fewer through his first 18 career starts, and seven consecutive strikeouts to begin his Sept. 1 start tied an AL record. Despite the White Sox's concerns about his workload, which increased over the course of the summer, Crochet maintained elite underlying skills, even if his 5.12 second-half ERA belied his talent. The Red Sox acquired him with the hopes he can further blossom into their staff ace. Considering his arrow pointed nowhere but up for the entirety of 2024, there's reason to believe he will. Crochet is a building-block pitcher for fantasy purposes.

Butler used up his rookie eligibility in 2023 and had a .582 OPS in 42 games, but he was electric during his first full MLB campaign last year with 22 homers, 18 steals and a .262/.317/.490 slash line in 125 contests. He still endured some ups and downs, however, as he was demoted to Triple-A in May after posting a .555 OPS through 121 plate appearances. Butler rejoined the Athletics in mid-June and was one of the best hitters in baseball the rest of the way, and he clubbed 20 home runs in his final 84 games. The underlying numbers back up the production, so there shouldn't be any major worries about regression in 2025. Butler clearly has the potential to deliver a 20-20 campaign, and the move from The Coliseum in Oakland to the more hitter-friendly Sutter Health Park in Sacramento should help him build on the breakout season.

Batting average used to be the ultimate measure of a hitter, but times have changed. Arraez, the three-time reigning batting champion, is now often referred to dismissively as a one-trick pony by fans and fantasy players. That may seem harsh, but there is no getting around the fact that Arraez's batting averages have been empty. Real GMs have found themselves coming to terms with his limitations as a player, with Arraez having already been traded twice and also mentioned in the rumor mill this winter. He added a little bit of speed last season, but Arraez has reached double-digit homers only once, and a low walk rate drags down his OBP. Helping his case is eligibility at both first base and second base entering 2025.

Raleigh set new personal bests with 34 home runs and 100 RBI last season, finishing as the No. 2 catcher in traditional fantasy leagues despite a .220 batting average. The switch-hitting backstop has become a folk hero of sorts in Seattle with his majestic homers and timely hitting among other reasons. The fact that he's a significant plus behind the plate with his defense and framing helps Raleigh's chances of approaching or exceeding 600 plate appearances for the Mariners once again in 2025. The drain in batting average is significant but does not negate the value of his power and counting stats, which get a scarcity bump in two-catcher formats. Expect more of the same in 2025 with Raleigh overcoming the pitcher-friendly skew of his home ballpark.

From a pure baseball perspective, it's a shame that Trout's career has trended downwards from one-time contender for "best player in baseball history" to merely a certain first-ballot Hall of Famer. Injuries have been a persistent problem for him across the last eight seasons, but especially the past four, during which he has missed more Angels games while on the IL (360) than he has played (266). Those ailments, and probably also the aging curve (he's now 33) have diminished his once-blazing speed as well as begun to erode his top-shelf contact quality. Even accounting for all that, Trout is still one of the game's most stellar talents. This guy, after all, hit 10 homers across his first 25 games of 2024. His power and patience remain his most marketable fantasy skills, ideal for points-based and sabermetric scoring, but Trout is more of a mid- than early-round pick these days with the many questions surrounding his durability.

Suarez made the most of his change of scenery and had his best season at the plate since 2019. That 2019 season will not be replicated, but for Suarez to hit 30 homers and drive in 100-plus in a neutral offensive environment with baseballs that were not traveling as far last year says something. Suarez continues to be a fastball destroyer and he remains quite capable of punishing mistakes. The third baseman still has a good amount of swing and miss in his game, which can lead to some serious peaks and valleys. To that point, he had just 10 homers and a .216/.302/.366 line at the All Star break last season. Suarez hitting 20 homers with a .307/.341/.602 line in the second half won some leagues and quieted the doubters who thought 2023 was the start of an acceleration into the aging curve.

Gausman wasn't quite himself last year after a bout of shoulder fatigue in spring training interrupted his preparations for the start of the season. The right-hander's velocity was down a tick in 2024 -- several ticks early on -- and the strikeouts dipped along with it. His surface numbers improved over the final two months, but the strikeouts never really rebounded, as he was below a 20 percent K rate in both August and September. Just one year ago, Gausman was treated as a borderline ace following a late-career breakout built on the strength of his trademark splitter. The market has perhaps overcorrected heading into 2025, though the massive decline in whiffs and tough division leave performance question marks and provide reason to invest elsewhere. Now 34, Gausman has two years remaining on his deal with the Blue Jays.

Turang is a throwback to 1980s baseball in that he makes the most of his speed. He is a pesky hitter who will work counts, fight off pitches and then put one into play, often to the opposite field, before turning on the burners. Turang plays within himself, realizing that double-digit homers are likely out of the picture most seasons, though his profile leaves him very much at the mercy of BABIP fortunes. Turang strikes out approximately once every five at bats, yet only Jake Cronenworth has a lower batting average over the past two seasons for all players with similar strikeout rates or better. The difference with most of the other names on the list is they make more consistent hard contact while Turang's contact metrics are all bottom 20th percentile. This profile fits at the bottom third of the lineup, leaving him plenty of chances to run but also making it difficult to reach even 80 runs scored.

Kikuchi's surface stats may not interest you much, but the numbers inside the numbers should. Before the trade to Houston at the deadline, Kikuchi was getting plenty of strikeouts with Toronto, but too many of his batted balls were landing safely and he won but four of his 22 starts. Upon acquiring him, the Astros encouraged Kikuchi to adjust his repertoire to throw more sliders and fewer fastballs, and the results were fantastic. The left-hander won half of his 10 starts for Houston while slightly increasing his strikeout rate and lowering his batting average against by more than 80 points. The next challenge for Kikuchi will be to find a way to reduce his home-run rate as he has allowed 25 or more homers in three of the past four seasons. A lower walk rate offsets some of that damage, but the long ball is what has kept his ERA above 4.00 in all but one of his seasons in MLB.

Adam has been on a three-year tear since being plucked by the Rays off the free-agent wire when the Cubs didn't see what they had. He has shown the ability to step in for saves when needed as well as contribute to all five pitching categories. Adam's success comes from his ability to throw four different pitch types to both righties and lefties, and he will use any of his pitches at any time. This past season saw him improve his slider which was downright unhittable. Adam's .162 batting average against over the past three seasons leads all relievers with at least 150 innings pitched over that span, and he is 10 points lower than any other pitcher on that list. Robert Suarez is still the favorite for saves in San Diego, but Adam has value as a late-inning weapon and his value skyrockets should anything happen with Suarez.

Few relievers made as many gains in 2024 as Jax. He added more than a half-mph to his average fastball velocity, significantly boosted the whiff rate on his sweeper and lowered his walk rate to 5.4%, with the result being the 10th-highest fantasy point total among relief pitchers (closers or middle relief). Jax thrived in his eighth-inning role, additionally securing 10 saves, and in most every regard outperformed closer Jhoan Duran in the process. That's not to say that a closer competition is destined this spring, but considering manager Rocco Baldelli's preference for matchups-oriented relief roles, Jax should put forth meaningful, nearly top-10 RP fantasy stats, regardless of how he's used.

Swanson's 2024 was a lot like his 2023 in many ways. His rate stats were nearly identical, but 40 fewer plate appearances and a lower spot in the lineup affected his RBI total. Swanson was clearly battling some issues health-wise since he immediately had core muscle surgery once the season ended in order to be fully ready in time for spring training. By and large, Swanson continues to stay on the field and produce in all the counting categories, but 2022 may go down as his peak unless the prevailing winds in Wrigley happen to blow out more than they blow in. The numbers around his plate discipline are rather stable if slightly unspectacular. His strikeouts make it tough to envision him hitting over .270 again unless he is blessed with good batted-ball fortune.

Effectively promised an everyday role with the Tigers after he signed a six-year contract in January, Keith had his moments as a rookie in 2024, even if his cumulative numbers appeared quite ordinary. He posted above-average contact, selectivity and raw speed metrics, and across one 52-game stretch around midseason, hit 11 homers with a .244 ISO to hint at prospective growth in that department. Long regarded one of the Tigers' top prospects, Keith should take another step forward in 2025, with a ceiling within the top-10 fantasy second basemen.

A consistently excellent all-around player despite playing under a relatively small spotlight in Cleveland, Ramirez should be a first-round pick in fantasy leagues of all types. He's the only player to have finished among the top 25 on our Player Rater as well as in total fantasy points scored in each of the past five seasons. In four of those, he finished among the top eight in each, and across that five-year span his 2,118 fantasy points were second only to Shohei Ohtani's 3,151. What's more, in 2024, Ramirez finished just one home run shy of becoming the second-oldest member of the 40/40 club (Barry Bonds, age 31, 1996), a signal that he still has plenty to offer fantasy managers. He's among the safest investments you'll find.

Chourio's rookie season is tough to appreciate until it's put into the proper context. He became only the 17th rookie in history to register a 20/20 season, with his .275 batting average ranking ninth amongst that group, and he finished 49th overall on our Player Rater and tied for 86th in fantasy points scored. Looking closer, Chourio began the season just 18 days past his 20th birthday, fresh off signing a record-setting contract for a player with no MLB experience, while also bearing a reputation for initial struggles when climbing competitive levels. He did stumble initially, with a .623 OPS through his first 67 games, but then he took off. Chourio's .309 batting average across his final 81 contests was ninth-best among qualifiers, and he scored the 11th-most fantasy points among hitters during that time span. The sky's the limit for this kid, who could very quickly establish himself as a perennial first-round fantasy pick in any format.

What a breakthrough Duran's 2024 campaign was! Few players have made as many all-around strides as he has over the past three years. He set personal bests in most every statistical category -- many of them by substantial margins -- culminating in his finishing 13th on our Player Rater and 18th overall in fantasy points scored. Most importantly, Duran, once a defensive liability, managed the eighth-best Statcast Fielding Run Value among outfielders, his strength in that department very much behind his MLB-leading 735 plate appearances. That amount of playing time will be tough to replicate, meaning some pull-back in his numbers is to be expected. Still, as a top-of-the-order Red Sox hitter, Duran should remain a top-50 fantasy performer regardless of format.

Rooker's arrival on the fantasy baseball scene has been quite unexpected. After changing teams three times during the course of 2022, he began 2023 as a platoon man only to burst forth with 30 homers. He followed it up with an even bigger breakthrough, finishing among the top eight in the majors with his 39 homers and a 16.6% Barrel rate in 2024. So where does Rooker, who signed a five-year, $60 million extension in January, go from here? The Athletics' move to Sacramento places them in a more hitter-friendly home environment for 2025, and the team's rekindled commitment to spending strengthened his prospects for a fantasy repeat. Even as a DH-only player initially, Rooker is well worth a mid-round pick.

Harris had a whirlwind season in 2024, going from a .304 batting average in the first month to a .200 average in May to landing on the injured list in June. His injury was classified as a Grade 2 strain of his left hamstring and the outfielder ended up shifting to the 60-day IL before returning in August. Harris ultimately bookended his campaign with an impressive month of September in which he slashed .316/.344/.579 with eight homers. He was regularly batting leadoff down the stretch and could very well remain there to begin 2025 with Ronald Acuna expected to miss at least the first month while recovering from knee surgery. A low walk rate threatens to relegate Harris back to the lower third eventually, but if he stays on the field he could finally reach 20-20 with Atlanta after falling just short in 2022 and 2023.

William Contreras finished last season on an island alone as the No. 1 fantasy catcher, but Diaz was right there in that second tier of earners just behind Cal Raleigh and Salvador Perez, at least in traditional leagues scoring batting average. Diaz finished fifth at the position in plate appearances with 619 and ranked eighth among all qualified hitters with a .299 average. It was an impressive showing after the Astros turned over the reins behind the plate, even if Diaz wasn't able to replicate the kind of power he showed as a rookie in 2023. In fact, Diaz hit seven fewer homers in 44 additional games. Nonetheless, Diaz established himself further and will be treated as a top catching option behind the younger Contreras entering 2025. Those in OBP leagues will likely want to bump Diaz down to account for a career walk rate of just 3.6 percent.

Few pitchers have ever possessed the kind of control that Kirby has shown. His 3.1% walk rate, through three MLB seasons, is already the lowest among pitchers with at least as many starts as he has during the modern era. But don't conflate that for a pitcher who peppers the strike zone with so-so stuff. Kirby's 96.0 mph fastball, slider, sinker, splitter and knuckle curve gives him a sound, consistently elite repertoire that should make him an annual candidate for top-10 fantasy SP seasons. In order to take the next step and perhaps score big Cy Young votes, he'd probably need to reintroduce his whiff-generating splitter of 2023, but even without it he's the kind of pitcher around whom you'll want to build.

Adames parlayed what was a career year on many fronts into a seven-year, $182 million contract with the Giants -- one of the offseason's earliest signings. He'll now play in a more challenging hitting environment than during his three and a half years in Milwaukee. Playing in the Brewers' HR-friendly home ballpark, Adames managed personal bests with his 32 home runs, 112 RBI, 93 runs scored, 153 hits, 33 doubles, 21 stolen bases, 74 walks and 282 total bases last season, while also pacing all major leaguers with 224 plate appearances and 93 RBI with runners in scoring position. The park switch assures some regression in the power departments, as does the good fortune in the RBI column. Nevertheless, Adames is a prime-age hitter who should put forth top-10 positional numbers in all fantasy formats.

Chapman didn't sign until March 1 last year, but he didn't let the late start affect him as he went on to achieve his best offensive season this decade. The third baseman popped 27 homers and ranked seventh in the National League in runs scored with 98. He added a speed element last season, swiping 15 bags in 17 attempts, which was rather surprising considering he stole 11 bases in his first seven MLB seasons combined. That said, Chapman is no statue and it's reasonable to think he could reach double-digit steals once again in 2025 considering the recent rule changes facilitating the running game and stolen bases in particular. The rest of Chapman's game looks fairly stable, including playing time given his excellent defense at the hot corner. Expect a relatively low average but useful counting stats in his age-32 season.

Suarez delivered in his first season as the Padres' regular closer, converting 36 of 42 save chances. It's slightly concerning that half of Suarez's blown saves came in September, a month during which he posted a 6.00 ERA and 1.50 WHIP. However, he shook it off and logged three saves in the final week of the season and then two more in the playoffs. Suarez's strikeout rate isn't dominant, especially for a closer, but last season his 6.2 percent walk rate was the fourth lowest among relievers with at least 20 saves. Suarez is the favorite for saves in San Diego, but last year was his first fully healthy season and he'll be 34 years old in 2025, so rostering setup man Jason Adam in tandem with Suarez may be a wise move.

Casas' combination of power and patience makes him a perennial breakthrough candidate, but through three MLB seasons, he has had difficulty staying on the field. An ankle issue cost him two months of 2022, delaying his arrival in Boston, shoulder inflammation prematurely ended his 2023, and torn cartilage in his rib cage shelved him for more than three months of 2024. Casas was also the subject of winter trade rumors, though he'll begin 2025 again as Boston's first baseman, hoping for better luck in the health department. At his best, he could challenge for top-five positional status in any fantasy league.

Though his control issues still crop up from time to time, Scott's skills have taken gargantuan steps forward over the past two seasons. Among relievers with at least 100 IP over that time, his 2.04 ERA ranks second, his 188 strikeouts rank fourth, his 69 saves plus holds ranks fifth and his .186 BAA comes in at seventh. Scott has also proven his durability by amassing the fourth-most relief innings over that time (150), something the Dodgers surely valued as they signed him to deepen their already strong late-inning relief corps. While the left-hander brings some volatility in the WHIP category, he should be a premium source of holds and/or saves. He should be one of the first relievers off your draft board once the proven, top-shelf closers are gone.

Garcia is coming off a career year in his ninth season in the organization since he signed as an amateur free agent in 2016. He earned the full-time spot at second base and hit all over the lineup over the course of the season. His lack of patience at the plate makes him better suited for the bottom half of the lineup, and as the Nationals continue to deepen their roster, it will become tougher for Garcia to get out of the lower half of the order unless some skills change. The good news is that he enjoyed his time down there last season, stealing 22 bases in 27 attempts despite just average speed since manager Dave Martinez has a lead foot on the running game. Garcia hit especially well at Nationals Park, slashing .329/.369/.549 with 14 homers at home compared to .233/.265/.335 with four homers on the road.

Rafael moved all around the diamond for Boston last season, making 87 appearances in center field, 82 at shortstop, 10 at second base, four at third base and one in right field. However, the Red Sox have since indicated that they believe the lack of a set defensive home may have had an adverse effect on Rafaela's offensive production, which was well below league average. He was briefly the talk of the fantasy baseball world in spring training, but Rafaela's success did not carry over into the regular season, as he fell in the bottom five among qualified hitters in OBP. Through it all, he totaled 15 homers and 19 steals in 152 games, which is impressive for a 23-year-old, even if it was largely volume driven. Center field will be Rafaela's set position for the foreseeable future and the Red Sox will be hoping he can settle in and finds his groove at the plate in 2025.

Rays manager Kevin Cash has a reputation for spreading the wealth when it comes to save chances, but Fairbanks has been the skipper's go-to arm in the ninth inning when available over the past two seasons. Fairbanks recorded 20-plus saves for the second straight year before a right lat strain ended his 2024 season, adding another chapter to his sketchy health history. Even with all the injuries in his career, Fairbanks continues to pump gas with 93rd percentile fastball velocity, though that didn't translate to many strikeouts in 2024. For now, Fairbanks can still be considered Tampa Bay's primary closer, but that run could be coming to an end in the not-too-distant future given his price tag for 2026 and the fact that he has incentives based on games finished in 2025.

Many drafters will seen Berrios' name and shrug before moving on to search for a player with more upside. Berrios is an old standby entering his 10th major-league season, but he is coming off an impressive 2024 season in which he won 16 games, tied for second in the American League. He has been consistent with his workload, making exactly 32 starts in each of the last six full MLB seasons, though the same can't quite be said for performance after Berrios led the AL in hits and earned runs allowed in a disastrous first full year with Toronto in 2022. That season shows a very real downside, but Berrios has steadied himself and once again looks like a viable if unexciting pick to help round out a fantasy pitching staff in 2025.

The Rays, as they are wont to do, flipped Eflin last summer after building up his value. Eflin was better than ever after his move to Baltimore, going 5-2 with a 2.60 ERA in nine starts down the stretch in the regular season after failing to replicate the success he had with Tampa Bay in 2023 prior to the trade. While Eflin does not have overpowering stuff, he keeps hitters off balance with six different pitches and is ultra stingy with walks. An 88th percentile chase rate suggests he could rebound a bit in the strikeout department in 2025. The team context is generally favorable, but keep in mind that the Orioles are moving in the left-field wall at Camden Yards, and pitching in the AL East is no piece of cake. With that, it's probably best to view Eflin as a pitcher that will be in and out of weekly lineups.

Baz began the season with Triple-A Durham, starting 10 games but only logging 39.1 innings. After being called up in early July, Baz started 14 games spanning 79.1 frames. His 3.06 ERA with the Rays looks effective, but a 4.39 xFIP and 4.33 SIERA paint a different picture. Baz's strikeout rate was way down while his walk rate was up relative to his pre-injury levels. Throwing 118.2 combined innings last season suggests Baz can handle a bump into the 150-170 range, and considering that he was able to reach back for more zip at times last season, it's reasonable to think he may be able to add velocity  in 2025. A return to pre-injury form and the top of the rotation is in play, but don't expect ace production right away.

Woodruff looked like a rising star for Milwaukee not long ago, earning All-Star selections in 2019 and 2021. However, he has missed the better part of two seasons due to injury, including all of 2024, after undergoing surgery in October of 2023 to repair the anterior capsule in his right shoulder. While the Brewers will not commit to Woodruff being ready for Opening Day 2025, he was said to be in a good spot and throwing multiple bullpen sessions per week in January. Entering his age-32 season, Woodruff is a wild card for both the Brewers and fantasy managers. The innings floor is zilch and the workload ceiling is capped, but Woodruff's excellent track record of performance (career 3.10 ERA, 1.05 WHIP) will likely tempt some to roll the dice outside the top 200 picks or so overall.

There was much expected of Jung after his smashing debut in 2023, but his 2024 never really got off the ground since Jung dealt with wrist troubles all season. He initially fractured his wrist the first week of the season after being hit by a pitch. Jung then missed over 100 games and rushed his rehab to get back to the club in July, only to wind up back on the IL three weeks later. Jung went on to have a second wrist surgery to relieve the pain he was still experiencing, but is expected to be 100 percent by the time camp starts in Arizona. It's been encouraging to see Jung's strikeout rate improve each season he has been in the big leagues, but the next step will be to accept more walks because he has been one of the more impatient hitters in the league, preferring to press the action rather than letting the action come to him. Jung is projected to hit in the bottom half of the retooled Texas lineup this season but could work his way up over the course of the year.

Greene, the No. 5 overall pick of the 2019 amateur draft and a top-10 overall prospect entering his 2022 rookie season, has made incremental gains across his three MLB campaigns to date. Unfortunately, those have also included extensive -- though generally unlucky -- absences, from the fractured right foot that delayed his arrival in Detroit in 2022, to the fractured left fibula that cost him five weeks of 2023, the Tommy John surgery that prematurely ended his 2023 in early September and the hamstring strain that cost him three weeks last summer. When healthy, Greene's contact-quality metrics are stellar, akin to those you'd expect from an All-Star. With some better fortune in the injury department, he could be ready to join the top-50 players in fantasy baseball in 2025.

Henderson followed up his unanimous 2023 Rookie of the Year season with a 2024 that saw him hit 26 home runs through the Orioles' first 80 games, second-most in the majors (Aaron Judge, 30), and finish fourth in AL MVP balloting. While Henderson cooled somewhat in the power department during the season's second half -- nine home runs and .174 ISO in his final 64 contests -- his cumulative numbers nevertheless cemented him as one of the game's premier shortstops, both for real life and fantasy. He's a centerpiece of one of the game's best up-and-coming offenses and a genuine, annual 35/20 threat. He is a building-block piece in both points-based and dynasty leagues.

Here's one of the most disappointing players of 2024, as his ADP in ESPN leagues was 18th overall, but he finished 55th on the Player Rater and tied for 170th in fantasy points. Rodriguez, only 24, has plenty of time to straighten things out.  Besides, his season wasn't a complete catastrophe, as he joined Mike Trout and Bobby Witt Jr. as the only three players in history to manage 20/20 numbers in each of their first three full MLB seasons. He also maintained strong underlying metrics in terms of his contact quality and raw speed, and he managed .295/.345/.486 rates, nine home runs and six stolen bases across his final 43 games after returning from a mid-year ankle injury. Rodriguez remains one of the game's most talented young players, albeit one who has shown a tendency for slow starts and is more of a rotisserie than points-based prospective star. He remains a strong early-round pick, especially in roto.

Devers is one of the game's more underappreciated raw power sources, probably in large part because he has never even placed among the top 10 in MVP balloting across eight MLB seasons. Nevertheless, he's the only hitter who can claim at least 30 doubles, 25 homers and a .500 slugging percentage in each of the past four seasons, during which time his Statcast average exit velocities and hard-hit rates have all rated in at least the 92nd percentile. Remarkably, Devers can claim that despite having been hampered by shoulder issues that cost him 11 of Boston's final 31 games and caused him to hit just .177 with one extra-base hit (a double) in the other 19. With a clean bill of health during spring training, he could be primed for a return to the 35-HR plateau. Draft him accordingly.

Alonso is 30, coming off a season with a career-high 42% ground-ball rate, and his free agency lingered deep into the offseason. All of this spawns concerns about his fantasy value that hadn't previously been present. He remains one of the game's premier power sources, hitting 34 home runs in 2024, making him the only player with at least that many in each of the past five full MLB seasons, but other aspects of his game have begun trending in the wrong direction. In the right environment, Alonso might yet have more seasons within range of his 2022-23 output in his bat, but his downside is beginning to deepen. Consider him to be an early- to mid-round pick, but he's no longer the fantasy building block he once was.

Between the addition of a splitter and some good fortune on batted balls as well as in stranding runners, Miller took a huge step forward during his sophomore season. He finished among the top-50 overall players both on our Player Rater as well as in fantasy points scored, and even posted 10 quality starts, a 1.75 ERA and an 0.84 WHIP over his 13 second-half starts. Considering Miller's strand rate placed second, his BABIP sixth and his HR/FB percentage ninth during that latter stretch, regression should be expected as he enters year No. 3. His splitter, however, gives him a more legitimate out pitch, and his control is strong enough that he should cruise his way to a top-40 SP season even if his ratios take a step backwards.

Nola is only a one-time All-Star, with his lone All-Star appearance coming back in 2018. While he may not receive much attention nationally, Nola is one of the game's most dependable arms, having made at least 32 starts in each of the last six full MLB seasons. He shaved almost a run off his ERA in 2024 and fell just three strikeouts short of reaching 200 Ks for the sixth consecutive full season. His knuckle curve remains an excellent swing-and-miss pitch and his four-seamer was more effective last year, as opponents combined to bat just .168 against the offering. The right-hander can get bit by the long ball on occasion, and in fact Nola led the National League in homers allowed last season. That said, he still does so much well and won't turn 32 until June. Until further notice, Nola should be considered one of the best No. 2 starters in baseball.

Diaz's first season back following right patellar tendon surgery looked shaky on its surface, but his underlying skills nevertheless had the look of a top-shelf closer. A trio of hideous early-season outings bloated his ERA, and a shoulder impingement cost him a few weeks shortly thereafter, but across the season's final three-plus months he had 15 saves (with a 2.41 ERA) and he tied for 11th in RP fantasy points. A winter of rest could do a world of good for Diaz, granting him a full ramping-up process and typical spring training. He'll return as the Mets' closer, a role from which he has twice struck out 90-plus hitters and twice saved 30-plus games (and don't forget he also had one season of each with the Mariners). He should be drafted among the first at his position in fantasy leagues.

Outside of an oblique strain that cost him five weeks late last season, Walker has been an almost spot-on, 30-HR, 90-RBI, top-eight fantasy first baseman across the past three years. His combination of power, patience and strong defense makes him one of the on-field game's most reliable first basemen, and one of fantasy's most consistent at the position. During the offseason, Walker signed with the Astros, where Daikin Park's Crawford Boxes should prove an enticing target for his pull-oriented swing (64 of his 95 homers from 2022-24 were pulled). Expect similar production from the 34-year-old in 2025.

Robert strained his hip flexor a week into the 2024 season and missed close to two months as a result. The outfielder struck out in nearly one-third of his 425 plate appearances last season and his power completely evaporated down the stretch, as Robert didn't hit a single homer in September and only popped three home runs in total after the All-Star break. It appears Robert, 27, will be given a chance to rebuild his value and audition for other teams as an everyday player on the South Side to begin 2025, and he had 38 homers and 20 steals as recently as 2023. The injury history and shaky plate discipline give him a wider range of outcomes than most, but Robert is an impressive athlete with obvious bounce-back potential.

Following a December trade from Miami to Texas, Burger is projected to open the 2025 season as the Rangers' primary first baseman, replacing Nathaniel Lowe. Burger totaled 579 plate appearances last season around an early stint on the injured list with an intercostal strain, falling one home run short of reaching 30 for the second straight year. He has had to deal with a lot in his young career, including two tears of his left Achilles' tendon during his time in the minors, along with a pair of trades. While he's a rather one-dimensional player, Burger hits for enough average -- exactly .250 the last three seasons -- to complement the power and make him worthwhile in traditional fantasy formats. Those in OBP leagues will likely want to downgrade Burger given that he's allergic to walks (career 5.7 percent).

A three-homer game during the second full week of the season set the tone for Langeliers' 2024 campaign, as he finished second on the team to Brent Rooker in both home runs and RBI with 29 and 80, respectively. Langeliers cut a couple points off his strikeout rate which helped lift his batting average from .205 to a slightly more palatable .224. Slugging will have to carry Langeliers' offensive game since he has a strikeout rate of nearly 30 percent for his career, and the Athletics' move to a Pacific Coast League park in West Sacramento should help in that regard in 2025. Even with the low average and limited time at DH to boost his stats, Langeliers will likely be drafted as a top-10 catcher in many leagues.

A cornerstone of the Nationals' rebuild, Crews, the No. 2 overall pick of the 2023 draft, has all of the tools necessary to develop into an eventual rotisserie and points-based fantasy star.
