His contact-oriented swing and blazing speed were most apparent during his 2024 MLB debut (albeit more rewarded in roto formats), but his contact quality metrics bodes well for his eventually adding enough power to help more in points leagues. Crews will need to curb his 56.4% ground ball rate in order to truly break through, but he's off to a good start to his career. He warrants a mid-round selection in redraft leagues and is a near-building block selection in dynasty formats.

Stott now has three big-league seasons under his belt. He has the skills and athleticism to hit higher in the lineup for another team, but it will be for him to crack the top third of the Philadelphia order while Kyle Schwarber, Trea Turner and Bryce Harper are healthy. If stuck in the nine hole, his RBI chances will remain limited. Stott is one of just three second basemen to register double-digit homers and steals in each of the past three seasons, joining only Jose Altuve and Mookie Betts. Stott contributes across the board and some BABIP regression would help him recover some of the 35 points in batting average he lost from 2023 to 2024.

After Devin Williams was lost for four months due to back issues and neither Abner Uribe nor Joel Payamps proved up to the role, Megill swooped in and converted 20-of-22 save chances, his 99-mph fastball and knuckle curve also making him a strong source of strikeouts. With Williams now in New York, Megill figures to get the first crack at the Brewers' closer job to begin 2025, from which he has the skills to be a solid second-tier fantasy option. His so-so walk rate and penchant for fly balls make him slightly riskier than the position's top-tier names, but he's well worth a selection in the middle rounds.

Pivetta has had his moments of fantasy greatness over the years, best exemplified on a cumulative basis by his having the 13th-most strikeouts across the past four seasons. Still, his hot spells have unfortunately been too few and too far between. Injuries, occasional wildness and an extreme fly-ball rate have been the obstacles standing in his path towards something more, though he did finish 2024 with a 3.92 ERA and a 29.7% strikeout rate across his final 14 starts. That gives some hope for a step forward. Pivetta did linger on the free-agent market deep into the winter, but so long as he lands a committed rotation spot somewhere, he'll be worth a mid-round pick with greater appeal in points league scoring.

One of the game's highest risk/reward players, Lewis has missed more Twins games over the past two seasons (172) than he has played during his three-year MLB career, yet in those 152 games played he has 33 HR and 104 RBI. He's still only 25 years old, with plenty of career left in which to shake his growing reputation for being injury prone, but at the same time, fellow Twin Byron Buxton had a similar penchant for absences that he was never able to shake. Lewis certainly possesses the ability to be one of the best at his position, but drafting him requires a leap of faith.

Chapman has not saved 15 games in a season since 2021, largely because of his propensity for walking batters, which is is too problematic for full-time closing duties. Yes, Chapman strikes out a high volume of hitters to offset his walks, but his walk rate has been at or above 15 percent each of the past four seasons. Walking a tight-rope in Pittsburgh is one thing; doing it in Fenway for half the season as well the other parks of the AL East is another. Boston also has other options such as Justin Slaten and the recovering Liam Hendriks for the ninth inning. Chapman's fastball velocity is still among the best in the league and homers are not as frequent as one might think. If Chapman could somehow get his walk rate back to a single-digit mark, he could once again be a high-end closer. However, that seems unlikely at 37 years old considering the fact Chapman has but once had a single-digit walk rate over the last eight seasons.

Singer, a first-round pick by the Royals back in 2018, was traded to the Reds this past November in exchange for Jonathan India and Joey Wiemer. The move from Kansas City to Cincinnati comes with a park downgrade, although it's not as significant as one might suspect, at least not in terms of overall run scoring. Great American Ball Park plays more favorably for power hitting, but Singer's heavy sinker approach should help mitigate that factor, at least in theory. He upped his strikeout rate last season and has shown decent swing-and-miss ability with his breaking pitches, though Singer's strikeout rate has typically hovered around league average. While he should be drafted as a streamer in 2025, Singer could emerge as a more regular option for fantasy managers if new skipper Terry Francona can push the right buttons and protect his leads.

Abbott was limited to 25 starts after his season ended in mid-August due to a strained shoulder, but he's expected to be healthy for spring training. His 3.72 ERA is misleading as shown by a less impressive 4.91 xFIP and 4.78 SIERA. A high 82.9% left on base mark rescued his season. Abbott's strikeout rate plummeted to 19.5%, down from 26.1% in his rookie season. His velocity and repertoire didn't change, so perhaps Abbott needs to be less predictable with his sequencing. He's slated to be in the Reds rotation, but unless he regains lost dominance, Abbott's ratios are vulnerable, particularly at home in Great American Ballpark.

Kelly's two-year run of success was derailed in 2024 by a teres major strain to his throwing shoulder which put him on the shelf from mid-April to mid-August. Arizona was happy enough with the results and confident enough in the health of his shoulder to exercise Kelly's $7 million club option for the 2025 season. He is such an unusual starting pitcher these days because his traditional fastball was his tertiary pitch by usage rate last season, with Kelly instead emphasizing his cutter and changeup. Kelly, like many pitchers in their mid-30s, has had to adjust his repertoire as his velocity has waned, and the changeup in particular has helped in recent seasons. The changeup to lefties and the slider to righties are his preferred put-away pitches, but his strikeout rate fell to below average last year around his recovery from the shoulder strain.

Friedl was limited to just 85 games last season due to a litany of injuries, beginning with a fractured his wrist in spring training. He also missed time with fractured left thumb and hamstring injury. Since 2022, the lefty-swinging Friedl demonstrated reverse splits, though 82% of his action has been facing right-handers. His Hard Hit and Barrel Rates are among the lowest in MLB, but a 45% flyball level yields power and a 15.2% strikeout rate usually keeps his batting average afloat. Last season's .226 average was deflated with an unlucky .229 BABIP. Friedl's defense is below average, so he needs to hit to play. He's ticketed to hold down the busier side of a right field platoon with Austin Hays, but if Friedl struggles, Hays can cut into Friedl's playing time.

Fresh off his unanimous 2023 NL Rookie of the Year campaign -- one that saw him become the first rookie in baseball history with at least 25 home runs and 50 stolen bases -- Carroll spent the first half of 2024 making a compelling case for fantasy bust of the year. A near-universal first round pick, he entered the All-Star break batting just .213 with five home runs, three of which came in the eight days leading into it, as he struggled throughout to adapt to swing changes he had implemented the prior winter. Carroll finally got it together during the second half, hitting .259/.351/.568 with 17 homers and 17 steals in 64 games, a welcome sign that the rotisserie superstar of old had returned. Just 24, Carroll would surely benefit from better luck on balls in play, but all signs have him returning to near top-10 form in 2025. It's just a year too late for those who drafted him that way last spring.

After a sluggish start to his Mets career, Lindor has recaptured his form as one of baseball's best all-around players. He has managed at least 31 home runs, 91 RBI, 29 stolen bases and 107 runs scored in both of the last two seasons, and showed decidedly improved raw power metrics. In fact, Lindor's strong finish to 2024 -- he hit .306/.368/.575 with 16 homers after the All-Star break -- hints at a possibly larger step forward in 2025. As the Mets made a big splash in free agency -- some guy named Soto -- Lindor's surging metrics come at an opportune time, as the team's offense should enjoy a noticeable boost from top to bottom. Lindor is a top-25 overall pick who, with some good fortune, could deliver first-round fantasy production.

Cease rebounded from a disappointing 2023 with a 2024 that, by many measures, was every bit as meaningful as his breakthrough 2022. Though his ERA (3.47) paled in comparison to 2022 (2.20), he set personal bests with his 8.5% walk rate and 1.07 WHIP. He recaptured the near-entirety of his lost fastball velocity, elevated his ground-ball rate to its highest number since his 2019 debut year, and averaged a near-identical number of innings per start (5.7). Best yet, Cease finished the year on a high note, posting a 2.58 ERA across his final 15 starts. He's also one of the game's most durable starters, having made at least 32 starts in each of the past four years. Cease is a bona fide fantasy staff ace and one well worth a pick in the opening rounds.

Cruz is making good on the hype and there is still room for growth as he enters his age-26 season. He cracked 21 homers and swiped 22 bags in 23 attempts last year, showcasing his loud tools and athleticism. There were some lingering issues with his left ankle after he missed nearly all of 2023 with a fracture, but the Pirates have said that they do not expect the ankle to be a long-term concern. The team moved him from shortstop to center field in late August, which seemed rather sudden at the time although it was not entirely unexpected given Cruz was always an anomaly as a 6-foot-7 shortstop. A strikeout rate over 30 percent for his career gives him some downside in batting average, but optimists can reasonably dream on another level of upside in home runs and stolen bases in 2025.

Clase is the quintessential example of why fantasy managers shouldn't put too much stock into postseason performance. The regular season's most dominating closer -- his 469 fantasy points were 43 more than the next-closest reliever and his 0.61 ERA was third-best in history among pitchers with at least 50 IP -- he was touched up for two losses, one blown save and a 9.00 ERA across seven October appearances. Chalk that up to a pair of ill-placed sliders and an Aaron Judge wall-scraper, as Clase's 100-mph cutter and slider are otherwise typically next-to-impossible to hit. He's among the best at his craft, and, on a Guardians team sure to be scratching and clawing for W's yet again in 2025, he's as good an investment as closers come.

After four seasons serving as one of baseball's most unhittable relievers -- both his 1.75 ERA and .146 BAA from 2020-23 were easily best in the game -- Williams' 2024 swung his skill set into risk/reward territory. Back issues that plagued him late in 2023 resurfaced during spring training, costing him four months, but upon his return he hardly skipped a beat. Among pitchers with at least 20 IP following his July 28 activation, Williams' 43.2% strikeout rate ranked second, his 14 saves tied for fourth and his .133 BAA ranked 10th. The Yankees acquired him during the winter to take over as their closer, their confidence signaling more ?reward? to his fantasy calculus. If his back issues are indeed behind him, he'll make another run at the position's top spot.

Lopez is a legitimate frontline starter in Major League Baseball, if not quite a fantasy ace. The right-hander has been dependable, taking the ball 32 times and reaching 180 innings each of the past three seasons -- the last two with Minnesota. Always stingy with walks, Lopez shaved his walk rate to a career-low 5.3 percent last season, which helped him keep his WHIP below 1.20 for the fifth consecutive campaign. He has five different pitches, all of which can generate whiffs, though his changeup was not as effective in 2024. Regardless, Lopez found his groove in the second half, pitching to a 2.77 ERA in 81.1 innings after the break. While Lopez may not look like a particularly flashy upside pick, he misses enough bats and could easily return to All-Star status. He has often underperformed his estimators, though it's always possible he could have a year where the results beat the peripherals.

Helsley vaulted himself into the elite tier of closers with his performance in 2024. He led the majors with 49 saves, setting the Cardinals franchise record, after previously topping out at 19 saves in 2022. While known for his velocity -- he averages nearly 100 mph on his fastball -- Helsley leaned more heavily on his slider last season to tremendous results. He went without allowing an earned run in two of the final three months, leading to a 1.48 ERA in the second half. The right-hander had a forearm blip as recently as 2023 and there is trade risk in addition to the injury risk in his final year before free agency. As long as he's upright and in St. Louis, Helsley will be locked into the ninth inning, and trade concerns should be marginal since there are few teams for which he wouldn't close if dealt.

The most anticipated Japanese hurler in seven seasons, Sasaki makes the jump to MLB after four seasons of a 2.02 ERA and a 32.4% strikeout rate overseas, which included a 19-strikeout perfect game in 2022. Though his velocity dipped slightly in 2024, he made 18 starts and had 10 wins, a 2.35 ERA, a 1.04 WHIP and a 28.7% K rate. Sasaki should immediately slot into the Dodgers rotation with prospective top-10 fantasy value in each start he makes. The primary questions surrounding him are health- and workload-related. Can he blow past 100 IP and secure his place as one of fantasy baseball's premier starters? Or will 2025 serve a stepping stone to a future claim of that status over the next couple of years? Either way, Sasaki should be selected in the middle rounds of 2025 drafts. He's a 23-year-old building block in all dynasty and keeper formats.

The ?Pasquatch? is an underrated hitter, especially for points-based scoring. Coming off a 2023 that saw him miss more than three months due to shoulder surgery, Pasquantino joined Yandy Diaz as the only qualified hitters in baseball with at least a 45% hard-hit but no greater than a 15% whiff rate on swings, even if his rotisserie numbers weren't anything special. Unfortunately, further bad luck in the injury department still holds him back as he missed September thanks to a broken thumb. With greater luck in 2025, he has the skills and the prime-age status to become a top-five points based (and top-10 rotisserie) first baseman. Consider taking Pasquantino in the early rounds in points leagues.

The top catcher in all of fantasy baseball not long ago, Realmuto has fallen back to the pack entering 2025. He underwent surgery on his right knee in June and missed five weeks, which kept him under 100 games played last season. The big problem, presumably related to the knee, is that he went from 16 steals in 2023 to a mere two last year. He can still hit for impressive pop, but speed from the catcher position was such a big part of his appeal previously, and while that aspect of his game may not be completely gone, it figures to be diminished in his mid-30s. Further, his walk rate has dipped in recent years, taking his on-base percentage along with it, and Realmuto has slid down the Phillies' order as a result.

Castellanos appeared in all 162 regular-season games last season before going 7-for-17 with a home run in the NLDS. By all accounts, he is well liked in the clubhouse, but despite all that, the Phillies have made it known that Castellanos is available via trade. So far, no move has gone down, but it is clear how the organization sees Castellanos at this stage -- not a great fit on a contending roster. The issue is his porous and only deteriorating defense in right field, which largely negates the value provided by his bat. As he enters his age-33 season, Castellanos is at risk of losing playing time, even if he stays in Philadelphia, give that he has not been a significant net positive in real life in any of the past three seasons. His 2025 fantasy value will depend entirely on whether or not he can maintain similar volume throughout the campaign.

One of baseball's best contact hitters, Hoerner has managed back-to-back top-80 fantasy seasons (in both roto and points-based formats) despite the fact that he hit just 16 home runs combined over those years. No, he's no power source, but his plate approach fuels a consistently solid batting average, his above-average speed and smarts on the bases make him a strong source of steals, and his status in the upper third of the Cubs lineup fuels a good number of plate appearances and runs scored. Hoerner's biggest knock entering 2025 is that he's coming off October flexor tendon surgery, which could threaten his Opening Day status. If he's looking good in March, however, he's one of the game's more underrated players, and well worth an early-round pick.

On the mend from his second career Tommy John surgery -- his first was in college in 2016, while this one was in August 2023 -- McClanahan should be eased back into the rotation gently by the always cautious Rays. Before the operation, he had developed into one of the game's best at his craft, with his 3.02 ERA and 33.4% whiff rates both ranking top-10 among pitchers with at least 50 starts from 2021-23. Whether McClanahan can quickly snap back to those levels is unclear, but if he's looking good during spring training and on track for the Opening Day rotation, he'd be a potential top-30 fantasy starter.

Estrada was a fantasy sleeper for a couple of years, but after he punched out 13 hitters in a row last May, everyone's eyes were wide open. He proceeded to post an impressive campaign, helping the Padres make the postseason. Once the Cubs' closer of the future, the 26-year-old righty could be in line to fulfill that destiny with the Padres, though he'll have to wait with Robert Suarez slated for ninth-inning duties and Jason Adam next in line as the primary setup man. Still, Estrada will garner high-leverage work and has a chance to join the 100-strikeout club while racking up holds.

Even though Bibee's ERA in 2024 was half a run higher than his rookie season, he improved his strikeout and walk rates to the point his 20.1% K-BB% mark was the 13th best among qualified pitchers. His home run rate ticked up, but it was still below the league average. Bibee's four-seam fastball registered a -8.5 pitch value after landing at 6.5 in his rookie season. However, he generated more swinging strikes and threw it in the zone more often last season. Last year's Hard-Hit and Barrel Rates against were lower than his rookie season, but the BABIP on his four-seamer was higher, driving down the pitch value. Consider the oddity as something to monitor but not detract from his status as one of the top young starters in the game.

Once an on-base machine, Nimmo has seen his OBP fall from over .400 during his peak years to just .327 last season. His batting average fell 50 points to .224, ranking in the bottom 12 among qualified hitters, while his slugging dipped below .400. The outfielder still fell just one homer shy of his career high of 24 established the year prior, and he set a new career high with 15 steals in as many attempts. It came to light in October that Nimmo had been playing through plantar fasciitis since May, which explains some of the issues, though if it was such a hindrance, it doesn't make much sense that he was running more than ever. Regardless, Nimmo is now something of a wild card entering his age-32 season given the sudden decline in rate stats. The Mets signed him to an eight-year extension prior to the 2023 season and will be hoping for a bounce-back campaign.

Shaw, the Cubs' first-round pick in the 2023 amateur draft, enters 2025 as a strong candidate to start at third base on Opening Day. After setting Maryland's all-time home run record (53), he managed .357/.400/.618 rates, eight homers and 15 steals across 38 minor league games in his pro debut, then followed it up with a 21-HR, 31-SB 2024 in which he acclimated himself well in 35 season-ending games of Triple-A ball. Shaw's well-rounded skill set appeals to any fantasy format and, while his speed might be his most bankable immediate tool, he could quickly develop in the power department. He's a dynasty building block and a late-round flier, even in ESPN standard redraft leagues.

After struggling with home runs and the command of his fastball as a rookie, Bradley made big strides in 2024 that bode well for his future. He boosted his ground-ball rate by 6%, added more than 2% to his whiff rate, and rattled off a final 20 starts in which his ERA was 3.71 and he generated MLB's 11th-most strikeouts (122). Considering Bradley's prospect status, it was a signal that he might begin to realize his future ace potential in 2025. The Rays do tend to take a conservative approach with their young starters' innings, and their move from pitchers' heaven Tropicana Field to George M. Steinbrenner Field sets them back slightly. Still, Bradley should be drafted in the middle rounds based upon his upside.

A decently regarded prospect back in his Dodgers/Athletics days nearly a decade ago, Holmes finally reached the majors last June at the age of 28, parlaying his elite control and whiff-generating slider and curveball into a swingman role with the Braves. His performance impressed them enough that he earned the start in their must-win Game 162 against the Mets, in which he tossed four shutout innings of 1-hit, 7-K baseball, and winter chatter had him as a likely member of their 2025 Opening Day rotation. Whether Holmes, who before last season's 109 1/3 combined innings between the majors and minors hadn't exceeded 90 frames since 2017, has the stamina to hold up to a full-season starter's role is in question, but he's an intriguing flier in deep mixed and NL-only formats.
